speechtext:
Hon. J. L. II.SI.EY (Acting Prime Minister) : I should like to make a brief statement to the house regarding the dispatch of a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to Windsor.
On Monday of last week, the premier of Ontario came to Ottawa to discuss the situation at Windsor. He stated that, with the approach of colder weather, the provincial government was increasingly concerned about the protection of life and property in and around the Ford plant at Windsor. Particular anxiety was felt as to the danger of fire. During the course of discussions which were continued over on Tuesday and Wednesday by telephone, Mr. Drew asked for an assurance that, if the provincial government, in pursuance of its responsibility for the preservation of law and order, requested the assistance of the R.C.M P., such assistance would be forthcoming.
The responsibility for deciding that additional police protection was required would be taken by the provincial government, and once the province had taken that responsibility, we felt it wou'ld be the duty of the federal government to furnish what assistance we were in a position to afford. Mr. Drew was accordingly given the assurance he requested.
An official request for a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to support the Provincial Police was received from the attorney general of Ontario on Friday and the request was complied with immediately.
Hon. members will have noticed the exchange of telegrams -between the attorney general of Ontario and the mayor of Windsor published in the press to-day. In Mr. Blackwell's message to the mayor he is quoted as stating that "Police action if taken will not be taken in relation to the issues between employer and employee in the strike nor will action be taken to prevent peaceful picketing.
I point that out to indicate that the action of the provincial authorities which the federal government supported was not, in any sense, intervention in the strike but was solely for the maintenance of law and order and the protection of life and property.
In the event of a request by provincial authorities for the dispatch of additional police in a case of this kind it is not the usual practice for the federal government to look beyond the provincial request. At the
Ford Motor Plant Strike

same time, the house, I am sure, will be interested in the information which has been furnished to the federal government as to the reality of the fire hazard which occasioned particular concern to the province.
I shall now read a copy of a letter from the Canadian Underwriters' association to the attorney general for Ontario, dated November 1, and a letter from the Canadian Underwriters' association to the premier of Ontario, dated November 2, copies of which were sent to the Minister of Justice in this government. The letter to the attorney general for Ontario is as follows:
November 1, 1945.
The Honourable the Attorney General tor the Province of Ontario,
Parliament Buildings,
Toronto, Ontario.
Re-Ford Motors of Canada Limited, Windsor, Ontario
Dear Sir:
This association, through its sprinklered risk department has had to issue a bulletin to its members which reads in part as follows:
"The plant (of the Ford Company at Windsor) is entirely without fire protection. The fire pumps are out of commission, the gravity tank has been drained, the sprinkler systems have been drained and watchman's patrol service has been cut down to one supervisor and four men per shift.
"The fire alarm system is out of commission, and all lighting and power circuits throughout the plant have been disconnected. All yard hydrants are without water and the only protection at the moment is from inside chemical extinguishers. If the strike continues, these extinguishers will have to be emptied, otherwise the contents will freeze.
"We wish to draw your attention to the fact that there are in the basement, 5-storey office building, many hundreds of sprinkler' heads, which are pendant. These pendant nipples have not been drained, and apparently the union objects to men being assigned to do this. If severe weather conditions prevail, there is every chance that the water in these pendant nipples will freeze, which may result in the rupturing of the fittings, with cpnsequential damage to the ceiling and other equipment."
The situation is one of very serious concern not only for the insurance companies directly interested but also for all fire underwriters doing business in Canada.
Unless protection is afforded forthwith, a fire loss of calamitous proportions can readily occur. The insurance coverage on this particular plant amounts to $35,000,000.
In stressing the concern of the underwriters we would wish to respectfully draw to your attention that this association fully realizes that it is not called upon to take sides in the dispute between the owners and the employees, or to consider the merits of their respective contentions. They are, however, vitally interested in the fact that there is no protection at the plant and that they, as innocent third parties, might have to bear a tremendous loss. They definitely feel, therefore, that they are entitled to call [Mr. Hsley.l
upon the attorney-general of this province to see that the plant is protected against the fire-risk. This lack of protection has nothing to do with the rights of the -workmen to strike or can it have any legal bearing upon the settlement of the dispute. It must, however, be noted that if a serious loss occurs, quite apart from the exceedingly heavy pecuniary loss, workmen will be without employment for a long time to come.
This association, therefore believes that not only in the interest of its members but equally in the interest of the general public and of the workmen of Windsor, steps should be taken forthwith to ensure that the maintenance men who could reinstate the fire-fighting apparatus and all other protective equipment should be immediately allowed to return to the premises.
It might be well to note that a continuation of the present situation in this and possibly in other plants under similar circumstances would lead to a disruption of the present insurance rate structure and consequential heavy imposts upon the premium paying public of Canada.
In view of the foregoing this association is* bound to respectfully call upon the government of this province to take immediate steps to remedy the situation and to grant adequate protection at the plant in order that all necessary maintenance staffs be permitted to enter and leave unmolested.
Yours very truly,
J. O'Brien,
Manager.
The second letter is as follows:
November 2, 1945.
The Honourable George Drew, K.C.,
Prime Minister of the Province of Ontario,
Parliament Buildings,
Toronto, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
This association has written to the Honourable tha Attorney-General for the province of Ontario as per copy of letter annexed.
The situation is one of great danger and the necessity of immediate action to protect the plant against fire hazards cannot possibly be overstressed. A loss, under present circumstances, could involve the payment of $35,000,000 by the association members. It would also mean lack of employment for thousands of men in Windsor for a very long period of time. -It -is respectfully and urgently requested that steps be immediately taken to' afford protection to the maintenance men who should be allowed to reenter the plant in order to prevent the occurrence of an event which would be disastrous for the city of Windsor and the province of Ontario.
Yours very truly,
J. O'Brien,
Manager.
I asked the superintendent of insurance to make further inquiries to-day to find whether the situation had changed and to bring the report on the situation down to date. He made inquiries, I think of the Canadian

Criminal Code
Underwriters' association, and as a result has sent me a memorandum which reads in part as follows:
Strike conditions have greatly increased the liability of the property to damage by fire.
Two elevated gravity tanks, the company's private water supply, and the yard hydrants are out of commission.
The entire plant is without protection except such as the Windsor brigade can afford but the distance from city water is so great and the mains are so small for a plant of this size that it is almost useless.
The only protection at the present time is fiom extinguishers but there is no heat on in the plant so that these are in danger of freezing and will have to be drained soon. All hand hose connections are now useless; there is no heat, light, power, or domestic water in the plant. The electrical alarms are all out of commission; the normal staff required to maintain protection in the plant is about forty men per shift, or 125 men in all, and this has now' been reduced to one supervisor and four men.
The plant's fire department and patrol cars are out of commission.
A big coal handling bridge is in danger from a pile of burning coal and the heat may buckle the bridge. The bridge is insured but the burning coal is not insured.
A gas reservoir with a capacity of one-half million cubic feet is water sealed and is now without any heat to prevent freezing; freezing may rupture the sides and allow the gas to escape.
I might also inform the house that the premier of Ontario called me by phone and suggested that perhaps something could be accomplished in the settlement of this dispute if the minister of this government would accompany a minister of his government to Windsor to see whether something could bp done. I suggested that the premier of Ontario support his telephonic request by a telegram, and I understand that a telegram came in after I entered the chamber, and I have not had an opportunity of seeing it. If the premier of Ontario in his telegram makes a request in accord with the request he made by telephone, this government will be prepared to have the Minister of Labour accompany a minister from the Ontario government to Windsor to see whether anything can be done, even at this stage, to settle the dispute.

speechtext:
Section 124 of the criminal code makes it an offence to point at another person any firearm or air gun without lawful excuse.
Criminal Code

The purpose of this amendment, which adds two subsections to section 124, is to make it an offence to print, publish or import, sell or distribute, magazines on the cover of which appear pictures depicting the pointing by one person of an offensive weapon at another person, or the shooting with an offensive weapon, if the picture illustrates a hold-up, robbery, murder or other criminal act.
It is entirely wrong and detrimental to the morals of young boys that they should continue to be permitted to observe and study on magazine counters such scenes as are described in these two subsections, or that they should be encouraged to read the sort of literature contained in these magazines by looking at such pictures depicting shooting scenes which can only tend to educate them to think that there is nothing wrong in pointing a gun at a person.
It will be observed that my amendment relates to the gun-pointing pictures on magazine covers, which pictures usually are printed in flashy colours. I shall be glad to have the assistance of an amendment that will cover also gun-pointing pictures on the inside pages of magazines. More than one news-stand dealer has told me that the elimination of gun-poimting pictures would not affect adversely the sale of good detective stories.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated to the house on Friday that at the earliest possible moment a bill would be .brought down to amend the criminal code, in order to check the series of crimes and violence reported from many centres in Canada. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) the mover of this motion, courteously notified me of this application; I have had an opportunity of considering it, and will not need to delay the house further by examining the statement.
Before giving this ruling I have considered among others two standing orders to which I should like to draw the attention of the house: (a) standing order 31, (b) standing order 15.
(a) Under standing order 31, leave may be , obtained to present a motion for the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent.public importance. Paragraph 6, subsection (d) of same standing order reads as follows:
The motion must not anticipate a matter whicE has been previously appointed for consideration by the house, or with reference to which a notice of motion has been previously given and not withdrawn.
It is the duty of the Speaker to see that the order of the day is followed, as the hon. members have it before them for some time before the opening of the house, and have prepared their work accordingly. However, I realize that it is the privilege of eveiy member to avail himself of standing order 31 and to request that the business prepared for the day according to standing order 15 (business of the house) be set aside, and it is for the Speaker to decide whether it is of sufficient urgency and public importance to suspend the daily business in order to discuss a matter which is deemed urgent and of public importance by the hon. member. On this question the Speaker has not to decide whether it is urgent to settle the strike immediately in order that the workers return to work and the industry get back to normal conditions. As I said in this house some time ago, the only question which is before the Speaker is to decide whether it is sufficiently urgent and important to set aside the orders of the day-in order to discuss the matter for which the hon. member is asking the adjournment of the house.
My opinion is that if the hon. member will look at the programme before us to-day he will find that some other opportunity will be given to him this afternoon to submit in committee the question which he has just presented.

speechtext: On Friday night we had reached item 6 in connection with air services, and I presume we will begin at that point to-day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I attempted to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing what 1 consider a matter of urgent public importance. Mr. Speaker at that time pointed out that the matter concerning which I had proposed the adjournment might be discussed at this point. Therefore I now rise to make some observations.
May I assure the committee that I approach the matter with a good deal of diffidence. This afternoon the Minister of Finance read to the house a statement which I considered to be serious, urgent and important, setting out one side of the dispute at the Ford plant. It is regrettable at a time like this, when we have just finished a war which was supposed to have preserved certain rights, privileges and freedom to the people of this country, that we should find not far from the House of Commons, in this province of Ontario, thousands of men and women who stood on the production line, suffered and worked long hours, and all the rest of it, in order that we might defeat totalitarianism abroad, and all that it stands for. I say this is regrettable, although as yet there has been no declaration on the part of the government that the war is officially terminated.
In addition to that, a large number of the men who are on that picket line to-day at the Ford plant are men who went through Sicily, western Germany, and other campaigns, with packs on their backs, fighting for the right to live in this country. To-day, after a dispute which to my knowledge in the last seventeen months has been discussed in the house on several occasions, we find the Ontario Provincial Police, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, operating with the sanction of the national government in Canada, in there on a picket line starting a new war on the home front. I say that to me it is very distasteful.
I make this further observation, that I do not believe what is taking place to-day in Ontario could take place in any other province of Canada. To me it is reminiscent of thirty years ago, when there was no labour legislation in Canada, when the mine workers m Nova Scotia had to face the cavalry and ail the machinery of war of that time to establish a union with a right to talk to their employers. But to-day that could not happen in Nova Scotia, and I do not think it could
happen in any province of Canada other than the one in which it is happening. The reason for this condition is that Ontario has no labour legislation to which the workers of that province can appeal in the event of the development of a situation such as we now find at Windsor.
While I am not being critical of the statement of the Minister of Finance, he pointed out that while this matter has been the subject of negotiation, and while the legal machinery of government was being canvassed by the workers at the Ford plant, the federal government was appealed to by the government of Ontario, despite the fact that according to press reports the council of the city of Windsor were asking for a postponement of any ' decision on the part of governments to use police. It was asked that this action be withheld until that city council had the opportunity of discussing the matter, and of trying to bring about a settlement by negotiation.
Mr. Drew and company did not wait until Monday. Mr. Blackwell ordered the police in. And, mind you, that is when the condition became serious. The picketing at the Ford plant prior to that time was not mass picketing; I am informed by union officials it never consisted of more than' fifteen men at any time at any gate. There was no disturbance; there was no disorder. There were many ways in which officials could have got to the plant, were they desirous of doing so, without going through the picket line. I understand the river side of the plant is tunnelled, and there is free access in and out. They did not go in or go out that way. It is simply a matter of provoking a bad situation, and the first responsibility must be accepted by the provincial government; I wish to make that clear. Secondly, the federal government will have to accept its full share of responsibility for sending in the mounted police, because to-day in Windsor, instead of peaceful picketing, the possibility of bringing about a settlement bynegotiation has been seriously hampered by such action.
There is mass picketing there to-day-and I have gone through enough of these things to know that your chance of settling it now. without a whole lot of misery, heartaches and scars, will be pretty slim.
Away back, months ago, we pointed out in the house on several occasions that the fact that the Ford Motor company had abrogated its signed agreement with the union in the matter of grievance procedure showed a weakness in the national labour code. We suggested at that time changes in the code which would prevent occurrences of this kind. I have not talked about the province doing anything
Ford Motor Plant Strike

about it because I knew they had no legislation that has a bearing on this situation. I am reasonably sure that they are not going to enact anything that will protect the working people of the province in this kind of situation.
Failing to get changes in the labour code that might hav'e offset this occurrence, just a few days ago we discussed the matter in the house. We had been watching the situation and realized that it was becoming serious. The longer settlement was delayed, the more difficult settlement became. We suggested at that time that a controller be sent in. Mind you, the union officials had made the ieclaration that if the government sent in a controller they were prepared to go back to work the next morning. This would enable the plant to resume operation and the status quo would be maintained. Such a controller sent in by the federal government would have the prerogative of getting management and the employees together and trying to work out a satisfactory agreement. It could have been done at that time without very much difficulty. But it was not done, and I am afraid that this is likely to spread. Already there are thirty other plants out in that area because of the police intervention; that has drawn out that many more. You have added to the picket line. In addition, representatives of this organization right across the country- they are tied in with the Canadian Congress of Labour, which has approximately 30.000 members-are discussing this matter. I am concerned about my own end of the country, where representatives of the automobile workers' union are consulting with the mine workers' union in Nova Scotia. I may get a telegram to-morrow morning stating that they are going to stand next. You may get word from the west to the same effect.
I am telling you that organized labour in this country recognizes that the Ford strike is not merely a struggle on the part of the Ford workers for union security or for a slight increase in wages; it is an official demonstration of a determination on the part of industry in this province to. smash the unions and trade union agreements. Organized labour are not going to sit idly by and see that take place in Windsor, because they recognize it as the initial wedge being driven in, action that will be repeated throughout the country. We asked the government to take some immediate action, to accept some responsibility, to send someone in there with authority who could take charge of that plant and get the men back to work.
I am concerned about this matter spreading across the country, perhaps within forty-eight [Mr. Gillis. 1
hours. If there is a clash op the picket line, someone is going to get hurt. If there is a clash on the picket line and someone is hurt in Windsor, you are apt to have a stand right from Vancouver to Louikburg. The unions in Ontario are new, they are war unions, and perhaps they are immature with respect to fighting this sort of battle. Do not forget that in the other provinces we fought this battle many years ago. We know what is taking place. It is just a repetition of what we went through thirty years ago. They are that far behind in this province in the field of trade unionism. The rest of the organized workers across this country are going to stand and give assistance to the men in Windsor, both financially and morally.
This is an attack upon many of the things we thought we fought this war for, including freedom of association and the right to collective bargaining. I have heard lip service paid to it on the floor of this house. I am not surprised at the statements that were read this afternoon by the Minister of Finance. The people affected by that strike appealed to the government, but no action was taken. Then the insurance companies became afraid that $35,000,000 of insurance might be affected, and they appealed to Mr. Drew on the basis of the possible loss in money. In order to protect the insurance companies and private property, Mi-. Drew 'is quite prepared to promote civil strife in Windsor. I am very sorry to see that that action has been condoned by the federal government by way of lending assistance in the form of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
It is said that the police going in there is not intervention in the strike, that the provincial police or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police going in there has nothing to do with the basic issues of the strike. Well it has everything to do with it. You might as well say that the declaration of war on the part of the Canadian government against Germany had nothing to do with the war, that it. did not involve us in the war. There is a little war on in Windsor between the Ford Motor company and the workers of Windsor. The crucial issue is whether they are going to have the right to a union or not. They are fighting that battle themselves. The intervention of the police, no matter how you may try to cover it up or polish it np.ds intervention on the side of the employer, and it is recognized as such by those who are on the picket line to-day. It has strengthened that picket line a thousand per cent. It has caused tempers to flare.
I understand that this afternoon the Minister of Labour has gone to Windsor with a

Ford Motor Plant Strike
minister of the province of Ontario. It is unfortunate that they did not go down to Windsor months ago and take some action before this situation developed. My suggestion this afternoon, without saying any more about it, is this: Unless the federal government are prepared to do what we suggested in the first place, unless they are prepared to appoint a controller and allow the status quo to prevail; unless they send in that controller with the authority of the federal government to get management and employees together and work out a collective agreement-that is their own business-it will be difficult to have a settlement. That must be done if you want to protect property.
Do not forget that the action of sending police in there has jeopardized human life, which is much more important than the protection of $35,000,000 worth of insurance or the protection of this plant and equipment. Do not forget that every day the strike is on means a loss in wages, it means pinched stomachs for the women and children of the strikers who are on the picket line. Hundreds of the men on the picket line are men who offered their lives to protect the institutions of this country during the last four years.
In the light of the situation that has now developed and which may spread across this country, surely this is the time to send in someone with some common sense to try to iron this thing out with the union officials and the representatives of 'the Ford Motor company. We must recognize the fact that strife in this province may spread all over the country. If you want to protect the plant and equipment and insurance, the best thing to do is to settle this strike. They are not asking you to take sides one way or the other; they are asking you to send someone in who has sufficient common sense to work this thing out. Then leave the matter of wages, conditions and union agreement to the men themselves.
Neither the Minister of Labour nor the minister from che provincial government is going to get a settlement in there under the present situation. They cannot get at the thing to start with. They cannot talk to anybody there. The simple fact is that the situation has advanced to the point where they are not going to talk to you. As I have said, they have already made that proposal to you.
The Minister of Labour has stated in the bouse that he presented a four-point programme to them. There is no need of my going over that. He told us he never got a reply. My information is that the union officials, in consultation with the Department of Labour, were told that they could make suggestions about that programme. They sent back a four-point programme, but nothing was done about it. The matter has been poorly handled in all directions. In my opinion there is no way of settling it to-day except the way I have just suggested. I say this in all seriousness. It is so easy to start trouble, awfully easy, but it is awfully difficult to get out of it. I went through many of these things years ago. and I do not want to see anybody else go through them because I know what can happen. If that thing breaks loose at Windsor, and you try to smash that picket line, it will be a serious matter, and this government will be to blame, because once things get beyond a certain point you cannot stop it; people do not reason after that.
I am sorry I had to take up so much time, but I earnestly suggest to the Acting Prime Minister, in the light of his statement and of the situation that exists in Windsor at the present time, that instead of just allowing two ministers to go down there to meet a lot of people who are not in a frame of mind to talk to- anybody-let me say that I was talking to some of the union officials on the phone to-day and they made a declaration to this effect-let the government pass an order sending a controller down there and the workers will be back to-morrow morning; then let the employer and employees meet around the conference table and iron out an agreement satisfactory to all concerned. That is the only way in which it can be settled in the present circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this question I am going to try to clear up some confusion and some misunderstanding and a great deal of honest difference of opinion about union practices and union terms and their meanings. I find that in this house there are various members who know a great deal about labour and who use union terms and give them various meanings, and so in my allotted time I am going to endeavour to clarify that situation and give to the house a bird's-eye view of the present labour machinery and make a suggestion that I hope will be helpful.
I will start by defining what collective bargaining is. It is a bargaining agency elected by the employees and which is not dominated, coerced or improperly influenced by the employer in any manner, by way of financial aid or otherwise, and so it presupposes that it is based upon honest intentions on both sides and that there is good will around the table. It does not for a moment contemplate synthetic bargaining-that is, sitting around a table and one party or the other shaking its head from left to right. I make reference

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If it is not too long, why can the hon. member not give a synopsis of it anyway?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I read from the Ottawa Citizen of October 26:
Quebec, October 25.-Premier Maurice Duples-sis to-day told a delegation of Quebec labour unions affiliated with the Canadian Congress of Labour that he was "strongly opposed" to a national labour code. To surrender these labour rights to the federal government "would mean the destruction of confederation at its very base."
I think that puts the premier's position quite clearly. I understand that there may be some opposition from another province. In any event that is the position.
One of the other reasons that we find ourselves in the present position is that our machinery for settling disputes is lacking in the things which conciliation machinery requires. What we need above all else m addition to the laws on our statute books is an incorporation into the employment bureau and into selective service of conciliation services so that, under those circumstances, not only do we find the man a job, but we put him at work and keep him at work.
Let us get downlo the basic problem which' is involved. On the one hand we have the employees who wish to join unions. After all, what are they looking for? They feel that in joining unions they will have a greater amount of security than they formerly had. They feel that the matter of wages is paramount, because after all it is from the wages they receive that they are able to buy their food, clothing and shelter. But I think a great number of people take a very narrow view of this. Hon. members will recall when the average working day was ten or twelve hours, or perhaps some miners will remember when it was fourteen hours. We are now down pretty well to the eight-hour day. Our conception of wages however has not changed to a great extent, but it should change. The worker's conception of wages has changed. He looks upon his wages not only as buying food, clothing and
shelter, but as having an educational and cultural aspect, an entertainment aspect, an old age pension aspect, an aspect related to leisure. For that reason he wants to join with his fellow men.
On the other hand we have the employer of labour. Usually he is a rugged individualist, and in more instances than not he is a pretty benevolent fellow. He believes in free enterprise, and if you asked him I suppose he would say that he was living under a system which was enlightened self-interest. The men ask for union shop and the check-off, and the only way to attain that, they feel, is through collective bargaining. On the other hand the employer, having to submit to collective bargaining, can, if he likes, make that collective bargaining meaningless, as I have already indicated.
Now there you have two opposite schools of thought. I do not think it is necessary for us to' go into either camp. I believe there is a middle way, a way of compromise. I am not talking about opposing one side or the other. Each party has to give up something in order that differences can be settled, and so long as they come around the table with honesty of purpose and in good faith, it is not at all difficult to settle those problems.
In so far as the employer is concerned he naturally takes the position, "Why should I strengthen this union, whose views are diametrically opposed to my views? If they are a strong union, they become vigorous in their bargaining and get a better deal than I would ordinarily want to give them." For that reason he thinks it is in his interest to oppose them as much as he possibly can. On the other hand, the union employee has to protect himself, first against the reactionary employer, he has to protect himself against the non-union employee, and he has also to protect himself against rival unions, company unions-and I could give you a list of those which have been set up from time to time and have been declared illegal.
If there is a lack of union security in the shop, this is what happens, as hon. members well know. The union that is in the shop must not only hold its members but maintain their interest, and one way of doing it is by raising contentious questions and keeping them continually boiling, sometimes initiating disputes which might be otherwise settled, in that way hoping to improve conditions, to show that they are on the job. But in the shops which have union security you will find more often than not that the union is a very constructive and helpful influence. It not only promotes employer-employee relations, but it strives to improve

Ford Motor Plant Strike

efficiency, to increase productivity, to promote the amenities which the men are so anxious to have.
Here are definitions of some terms about which many of us find it difficult to be clear. We talk about a closed shop. A closed shop in the collective agreement means just this: It is an agreement between employer and employee whereby the employer may employ only members of a specified union. He usually does that through the business agent of the union. You see that kind of union, you have lived with that- kind of union for many years in this country without perhaps knowing that you have, because you have that in all craft unions in this country and in all textile unions. If you want a bricklayer or a carpenter you go to the business agent and he is the man who sends the bricklayer or the carpenter, and in the textile industry if you want a cutter or an endmaker you go to the business agent and he produces the man who is able to do the job.
One conception in this country, and I find it everywhere, is that these men are asking for a closed shop. Believe me when I say that the industrial unions have never asked for a closed shop. They do not want a closed shop, and if you gave them one they would not take it. What they are asking for is a union shop, which is altogether different from a closed shop. There is a closed shop in the province of Saskatchewan. There you have the closed shop and the compulsory check-off, . and that is the* ultimate in trade unionism. It is an experiment that is worth watching. It may be unfair to the labour movement generally in this country because it is being put on such a narrow basis. I merely point that out as an example. Perhaps also the narrow basis of the Social Credit experiment may have had something to do with the experiment itself. It may be fair or unfair; it depends on the way you look at it. Now the closed shop may discourage industry from going into Saskatchewan, or on the other hand it may have the effect of encouraging it.

I said the experiment in Alberta. I could not be so wrong. On the other hand, as I said, it may encourage the industry to go there. It is quite possible, and I know very little about Saskatchewan industry, that giving them a union shop and check-off is like giving someone a sleigh in Florida. It does not snow there. So far as I am concerned, I am very hopeful that it will be successful, and I hope it is encouraged. We will watch it.
I gave the definition of closed shop/ Let us tee what an open shop is, and presently we shall get to the union shop. Formerly an open shop was a shop where there was no agreement in effect and no union activities were permitted. To-day the definition has changed somewhat. The definition of open shop to-day is applicable to a shop where collective bargaining agreements do not make membership in a particular union a condition of employment, and it is open to union and non-union members alike. Ford had an open shop. Now a union shop-and may I for a moment bring you back to the difference between the union shop and the closed shop. The Union Shop Agreement permits the employer to hire anyone he wishes, but all employees must be members of the union within a specified time and they must maintain that membership as a condition of employment. There is another sort of -shop, and it is called maintenance of "membership shop, or irrevocable check-off. That is often recommended in this country; that covers all employees who are members of a union. It covers those who later becomp members of the union, and they must remain members of the union, during the life of the agreement, as a condition of employment.
Then of course there is the check-off about which we hear so much. The check-off may be either voluntary or revocable, and all it consists of is the signature of authorization by the employee and presenting it to the pay office, the company then deducts from the monthly earnings of the employee the dues belonging to the union and remits them to the union. The check-off is very important to the union, particularly in its early life, because it ensures stability of income; but it is merely a mechanical process.

As to the distinction between the closed shop and the union shop, I have tried to give you the kernel of it. The closed shop must hire members of a specified union. The union shop -may hire anyone it likes, but he must in time become a member of the union in the shop. Maintenance of membership covers all who are or become members of the union and permits non-union employees to share in the benefits of work on equal terms in the shop. The check-off is merely an administrative function, and whether it is a closed shop, union shop or maintenance of membership they all need it.
So far as the union shop is concerned, I too read Maclean's as to whether it is democratic or not democratic, and I was not impressed particularly by the people who had the affirmative. I do not think it is a question of fairness or unfairness at all. The real question is whether the injustice involved displaces a greater injustice. You often hear about take-home pay. That is a common term that is used and I suppose everyone knows it means -what the envelope contains when you take it home. Perhaps I can bring it home closer to us. We here receive $4,000 for our very heavy work, and after expenses are paid most of us may have a thousand or fifteen hundred dollars. That is the take-home pay, so the wages are not $4,000, but actually $1,000 or $1,500.

speechtext:
That is the money that buys the groceries. That is the way the worker understands it. You have also heard a great deal about severance pay. That too is a term that is used a great deal, and I can best explain it to you by giving an example. A corporation president suddenly becomes chairman of the board. Usually he has become ineffectual, and very aged, and usually they have had had to kick him upstairs, for a consideration.
There are certain clauses that are common to all agreements. You will find in every collective agreement a clause dealing with grievance procedure, how complaints should be handled, where the forms are, whether the staff will have time off and who pays for the time. You will find a clause dealing with the authorization of the check-off. You will find a clause dealing with the matter of discrimination by the employer, or coercion by the employee. Other clauses deal with seniority rights, with the rights of men from the armed forces returning to their jobs, or synthetic rights to those who have never had a job in the factory before.
There are various clauses which deal with complaints of employees who claim that they
are not members of the union, in which case there is a procedure laid down whereby the minister appoints a man who is the final arbiter. He decides, in the light of all the evidence, whether a man is or is not a member of the union. Usually there is a clause dealing with how contracts are to be renewed. Those are various things that they must agree on at the conference table.
Disputes arise in various ways. One of the not uncommon disputes is a jurisdictional dispute between two unions, perhaps the A. F. of L. and the C.I.O. union. They have an argument over jurisdiction. Sometimes you will have a dispute arising over recognition of a union; sometimes it will be on the question of conditions and wages, sometimes on the question of procedure, sometimes on the interpretation of a contract, and in the particular case which we have before us, on the question of union shop and check-off. Usually they are settled by negotiation. Where the parties are unable to agree in Ontario the Ontario regional board steps in, either sends a conciliation officer or hears the dispute and gives a decision. If that does not settle the dispute the dominion labour minister can step in and appoint a board, either a three-man board, or, by agreement, a one-man board. But none of the boards can do more than recommend; the employer may accept the recommendation or may not, and the same thing applies to the employee.
In the Ford case a board did sit and it made a recommendation. The majority of the board, two members out of three, recommended in. favour of the check-off. One member of the board recommended maintenance of membership and check-off, and the employers' representative just shook his head to all of them and said: "Nothing doing." If the negotiations fail, then, of course, there is an opportunity for voluntary arbitration. That is exactly what is being tried in this particular case; and if that fails then there is nothing left to do but just to slug it out. I need not say anything further about what should be the position of those people who stand on the side lines.
Our conciliation machinery proceeds upon the theory that one board will hear one dispute and the members of the board may not know anything at all about labour; they may not know anything at all about the question in dispute and they may never have sat on a board. But whatever findings they finally make are merely recommendations. As I said before, either side may refuse to be bound.
There are advantages and disadvantages to that procedure. I suppose it is advantageous to say that these are fresh men with fresh

viewpoints and that they are unprejudiced. Hon. members who have sat on such boards know that what usually happens is that the employers' representative and the employees' representative both make a plea for the chairman who is about the only unprejudiced man on the board. They are not tied to precedent and consequently travel along the road of trial and error. Therefore in time, by putting many fresh minds on the job, we may arrive at some formula. Of course there are some disadvantages to that too, in that there is no continuous development of union security formula in the various findings. In this house we are bound by precedent. Sometimes, if the precedent favours our idea, we think it is a good one; if it does not, we think it is a bad one. In any event we have something to go by, and if we do not like it we can change it. On the other hand, the conciliation boards are not bound by precedent and decisions vary. Sometimes you get a good decision, sometimes you get a bad decision; sometimes the decision will be merely patchwork, and sometimes it stops the bleeding for the time being.
After those decisions are made and neither party feels bound by it, there are still weapons in the hands of the various people. In soTar as the employees are concerned there is always the threat of a strike; there is always the threat of a slow-down, and, of course, there is always the strike which is the weapon of last resort.
I think the committee' should remember that the decision of the top executives rarely determines whether there should or should not be a strike. The decision is always made by the rank and file. It is an economic decision which men dislike to make. It is more fateful to them and to their future than that which led the members of this house to decide whether they could afford to run at the last June election. It is always a decision that, once taken, is seldom put aside.
The history of strikes is that strikes are seldom broken. If they are, all the employer gets from it is guerrilla warfare. In so far as the employer is concerned, he has some weapons in his hands. He can somehow get rid of the people he thinks are the trouble-makers. On the other hand, he can come to the table, sit around and shake his head, and in time the strike turns out to be a lock-out.
One of the great influences-and both the employer and employees are alive to the situation-is public opinion, because there is always a moral issue involved. In a strike usually the consumer is the sucker, because he needs the product of the business; his bread and

butter depend on it. Well, he sits by and seldom has a word to say. Naturally, we agree that that is morally wrong. But there is public opinion. Speaking broadly, the public never want to see the men beaten; they are always ready to give the men a little more than they had before, perhaps not all they want, but a little more.
I have made some investigation into the history of strikes in this province. The latest figures I have been able to obtain show that in the last fifty-five disputes we have had where there have been boards sitting, thirty-three of them have recommended the checkoff; twelve have recommended the union shop and maintenance of membership. These have all been majority recommendations. I point out these figures to the committee merely to indicate how the wind is blowing.
We often have these questions asked: Why the check-off? Why do they not have the check-off in England where trade unions are cock of the roost? As the committee knows, the union shops are old institutions in England. They are respected and cherished. Their growth has been gradual; they have been there for a very long time, and neither industry nor the employees would have it any other way. It is not fair to compare our new industrial unions with the old established unions of the old country. It is not any fairer to do that than it'is to compare their pub with our beer parlour. When our beer parlours start to prize their licences; when the people learn to drink and not guzzle beer; when beer starts to taste like something, perhaps it will take on a different aspect. But for the present it is hardly a fair comparison.
We must not forget that every day in the life of every employer in this country he carries on a check-off, because he checks off when he deducts taxes for the Minister of Finance. He checks off when he makes deductions for victory bonds sold to his employees. In welfare drives he does it again. All it requires is just another punch on a calculating machine, and handing over a cheque.
The employer who refuses the check-off to his employee is doing it, not in the interest of good employer-employee relations. I said before that the collection of dues was a problem of the highest dimension with the union, because it requires those dues in its very early stages; and it is necessary, no matter what sort of job the men may have. Unions are never satisfied without it-and unions are no different from any other group of people. They have delinquents, and the easiest thing to do is to take the amount off at the source.

Ford Motor Plant Strike
Instead of turning in our income tax returns at the end of the year, and then wondering whether w-e shall have something with which to pay taxes, the Minister of Finance has made the practice of making sure of our contribution by taking it off at the source. The union merely wishes to follow what it thinks is a fair, well established and fine practice. They want to take it off at the source, so that there may be no dunning of union members.
After all, these people are the same as we are. Many of us who belong to the Masons or the Knights of Columbus, the law society or the medical society, know that we have delinquents. If those organizations could collect their dues at the source they would like to do so.
In dealing with delinquents and union members with shortcomings, naturally the officials do not like to throw aw-ay the good will of the members. Of course they can fine a member if he does not pay his dues, but if he cannot pay dues he certainly cannot pay a fine. The only alternative is to expel such a member. At various times I have heard some talk about expelling members and depriving them of their livelihood, but that is-the last thing a union wishes to do. In twenty years of contact with labour unions and labour officials I have never heard of a man's being expelled. It would be a most unhappy experience for the union. In the final analysis, they just forget about it.
I think no one will quarrel with my statement that unions are a powerful force in our community, and not only that, but that they are a powerful democratic force. I do not think anyone will quarrel with me when I say that there are 45.000 industrial union people in Ontario, and that they perform a useful function in society. Usually they are behind victory bond campaigns; they are behind social problems, such as drives for social services. In the opinion of the labouring people, the unions are the only ones that can stand up, not to a benevolent employer but to a reactionary one. All that is asked of members of unions, in return for security, is that they give responsibility. As they become united, naturally they become more responsible. Up to date, the over-all record will show that they have nothing to be ashamed of.
But I point out to the committee something often lost sight of: If the employer would leave these industrial unions alone, and let them go about their business of unionism and the, administration of unions, instead of constantly fighting and harassing them, I think he would draw dividends.
What is happening to-day is that in fighting with the union they are keeping in office all the firebrands, and the union has not time to get down to the work of administration, and the important work for which the union is there to function. If the employers would only see that, they would realize that one of the most serious charges of irresponsibility made against union leaders can be remedied by action of the same employers.
Unions have also been accused of political action-and I do not think they deny it. On the other hand, I think most of us can search our souls and see that we are all somehow- responsible for throwing them into the hands of my hon. friends over there. Mind you, I would like to see them on our side-or at least more of them; but they were desperate. They were looking for friends in this country, and one cannot blame them a bit if they felt that they had friends in one particular camp.
If we are to get a full picture I think we ought to ask ourselves, a few questions, as we approach this problem. We ought to ask ourselves if it is a good thing for Canada to have such great economic power, in the hands of so few people. We must also ask ourselves this question: Is it good for Canada to have an industry which is built up on tariff walls, nurtured by our natural resources, provided with a pool of people, subsidized in times of unemployment by municipalities, the province and the dominion, an industry which, as has been pointed out in the house, has large swollen profits, which enjoys a virtual monopoly in Canada and which manufactures a product essential to the economic life of our country-I wonder whether a company, under those circumstances has a right in bad faith to refuse to bargain collectively, because it has. archaic views, or because of any particular pique.
I think the committee agrees that the w-brkers have no right to violate the civil rights of industry. And then, I ask the committee:	Has industry the right to impose
economic violence upon the workers? Can we afford to give Canadian workers less of the democratic processes and of industrial justice than do United States executives across the boundary line to men who do the same work, under similar conditions, making the same product and for the same company- with the exception that we in this country have the privilege of paying more for the product than they pay for it on the other side of the river?
If that is victory; if that is what we fought for, then V-E day and V-J day become meaningless, and many people in Canada will feel

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to follow the last speaker in the remarks that he has made. I would just like to point out that there is no need of suggesting that the government should step in. The government is in up to its neck, but in a way which in my opinion, it was not necessary to get in if it had got in a little earlier. I do not believe there is much use in discussing this subject unless we try to find out the causes leading up to this particular strike. It is regrettable that within little less than a month
after V-J day this company and its employees both of whom had such an excellent record of production during the war were fighting with each other. The plant is idle; the employees are out of work, and the manager, as far as I can learn, is sulking.
There should have been some way of bringing these parties together. In my opinion the responsibility for doing that rests upon the federal government, more particularly upon the federal Department of Labour. How did this happen? Some of the reasons were touched upon by the last speaker. In the first place because of the long-standing policy and attitude of Canadian employers generally of refusing to deal with organized labour. Hon. gentlemen who disagree with 'that point of view should read, if they have mot already done so, the May, 1943, report of the national war labour board.
The second reason for this state of affairs follows, in my opinion, from the statements made by the Minister of Labour prior to the election, that as soon as possible controls were going down the drain. Well, if controls go down the drain, something else will not go down the drain, and that is the relations between employers and employees.
The third reason-and I mentioned this when I spoke on another occasion in this house- is the tacit agreement of the government with industrialists to depress wages in this country. Exception was taken to that statement when I made it before, but I think I now have the proof. I have in my hands a report that appeared in the Vancouver Promnce, and, I imagine, in all the papers across Canada, of an interview on October 12 with the deputy minister of labour and director of national selective service, Mr. MacNamara, who is quoted as having said:
After three years of necessary "regimentation" Canadian workers will shortly get back freedom of action.
What sort of freedom of action do the workers get back? I will skip the rest of the interview to the last paragraph:
Mr. MacNamara said to-day that there are indications that high-paid war-time workers are beginning to realize that they cannot hope to command comparable wages at their former p .'ace-time jobs and are becoming reconciled to the situation.
Reconciled to the situation! Reconciled to the freedom of having to accept lower wages! That is the freedom the workers get out of the elimination of controls. He went on:
More and more men are returning to their former jobs. All the government can do just now is to keep workers infornud as to the number and type'of jobs available.

No wonder, with a condition of that kind facing the workers, that they make protest. Why could we not pay as high wages in ordinary peace time, after we had released perhaps 2,000,000 people from unproductive war work and had them ready for productive work? Why should the workers have to take lower wages? Why should the workers have to become reconciled to lower wages? That sort of talk just does not make sense. The greatest need at the present time not only in Canada but throughout the world is production, and at the very time that we need production we are reducing the rewards of labour and the means by which labour can purchase its increased production. As I said, it does not make sense.
I suggest to the go'vernment that, instead of fostering a policy of lowering wages in order that this country might compete in a mythical world market, they institute a policy of maintaining wages, so that they can put the people to work. The workers need incentives as well as do employers, so that they will be able to buy the products of their labour. That is the crux of the dispute in the Windsor plant.
Let us remember that the Ford plant was one of the last to accept the policy of collective bargaining during the war, and they really never did accept it except in a token sort of way, because when the strike came on September 12 the employees had been negotiating with the company for an agreement for seventeen months. The Department of Labour had sufficient power to take action to keep the employees and the company in negotiation until a working agreement was arrived at.
I have outlined what in my opinion are the basic reasons for this dispute and for other disputes that will come. Having stated the causes, I believe they themselves indicate the remedy. I would suggest that the Department of Labour insist, as it can insist, on the Ford Motor company entering into an agreement with its employees. The minister takes the position that he cannot take sides in this issue. I agree with him that he cannot take sides. But there is one thing which I thinlc the minister overlooked and which was stated by the previous speaker, namely, that there are three parties to every labour dispute: the employer, the employee and the public. The Minister of'Labour, if he cannot take sides, can at least keep the public informed as to who is responsible if a settlement is not made. There is nothing that he cannot do to keep the people of this country well informed as to who is preventing a settlement, the workers or the management. Once that is done, I think the situation will be made easier for the minister himself. So I suggest to the govern-
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
ment that, instead of either tacitly accepting or agreeing with employers for the reduction of wages, they start on a policy of maintaining wages and even raising wages in the lower income levels. Remember that wages were frozen in these levels during the wrar.
I have already referred to the national war labour board's report. In that report the board proposed that workers should be free to negotiate for increased wages where the rates were below fifty cents an hour.
I also suggest to the government that, in whatever way it can be done, whether through conference with the provinces or otherwise, they institute a system of compulsory collective bargaining; that is, making bargaining compulsory on both employers and employees. I am not now suggesting that the acceptance of findings should be compulsory: that matter can be decided later. I agree with the hon. member for Spadina that on these conciliation and arbitration boards we should have at least a chairman that has some understanding of labour-management relations. The hon. member mentioned a number of names. I should like to add another, that of a man who, I am sorry to say, gave up a position as chairman of the national labour board, which he handled very effectively, to enter politics, for which I do not think he was so well fitted. I refer to to Hon. C. P. McTague. I have had occasion to criticize him in this chamber, but never for his decisions in labour disputes. He had an understanding of the underlying philosophy applicable as between worker and management which is possessed by only a few of the judges whom I have seen on conciliation boards; and we need men of his kind.
I believe also that the government, in whatever way it can be done, should make union security compulsory where it is asked for by employees. It is a singular fact that very often Canadian companies which are branches of United States corporations refuse to accept in Canada labour conditions which are' in effect on the other side of the line. In this case what the workers of Windsor are asking for is in effect in Detroit. We had in Vancouver a strike by employees of the American Can company who asked for a union shop, which the company refused, although it was in effect in their plant at Seattle. I am glad to say that that situation has been remedied through an award made by Mr. Justice Richards.
There is one other point to which I should like to draw the attention of the committee. During the war the workers have had a few years of full employment and the economic security which goes with that condition. They

are going back now to a condition which Mr. MacXamara calls "freedom of action." which means freedom to work for a few weeks or a few- months, and the harder they work, the more they produce, the quicker they will be looking for another job, which usually is not there.
Before we can have industrial peace; before we can attain the state of cooperation in industry which is so much desired, we must do something which will remove that fear of unemployment from the mind of the worker.
It is not going to be easy. Remember that as our means of production improve and as we can produce greater amounts of goods with less labour in less time, more and more labour will be eliminated and permanent unemployment. will become the lot of an ever-increasing number of workers. I saw somewhere that the productive efficiency of industries in the United States increased twenty-five per cent during the war period, and I imagine that there has been the same degree of increase in Canada. If we do not raise wages so that the workers can benefit by this increase in industrial efficiency, we shall in no time be back to the depression of the thirties; a depression, let us never forget, not of scarcity but of abundance. This is the fear that must be removed from the minds of the workers if we expect to get their cooperation and avoid disputes such as we have to-day in the city . of Windsor and which may occur to-morrow in any city in Canada.

This debate is timely; in fact we should have had it a long time ago. The Ford strike question is one of property and civil rights and, therefore, a provincial responsibility. The provincial authorities of Ontario have argued that the dominion government took over, through the War Measures Act, and propose to retain, through bill No. 15 which is now on the order paper, the power to deal with industrial disputes such as that now raging in Windsor. The Minister of Labour has not clarified the situation. This, I believe, is one of the greatest mistakes he has made. I have high respect for him, but I believe he has cheapened himself and greatly lowered his prestige throughout the country by a vacillating attitude, acting as though he did not dare take a stand in this most important matter. No other member of the federal government has clarified the situation. Consequently the constitutional aspects of the matter are not generally known in the country. I understand that the Ontario government through Mr. Blackwell has declared that the dominion government has the authority which ordinarily the
provincial government would have, this authority being that of the federal government under the War Measures Act. The dominion government has not conceded that fact, so that the whole situation is in a most unsatisfactory light.
Under the War Measures Act, just what is the situation as to the power to act in connection with industrial disputes? Has the federal government the authority and the responsibility to deal with this question, or has the Ontario government that authority?
I think the very first requisite is to clarify that situation. Unquestionably this Ford strike has to do with property and civil rights and it is, therefore, unchallengeably a provincial affair. If the dominion government has taken full responsibility through the War Measures Act and proposes to continue it through bill No. 15, then let everyone know, and we shall know immediately where to pin the responsibility and of whom to demand the results.
Something else that is very vague is . the question, just what is the policy of the dominion government and what is the policy of the Ontario government? Does the dominion government through the federal Minister of Labour favour the principle of union security, or does it not? If the federal government would make a clear-cut statement everyone would know where we stand, but it seems to me that once more the government is vacillating and shifting in an unsatisfactory manner, and by adopting that policy it is contributing to the gravity of the situation confronting Canada to-day.
Where does the Ontario government stand with respect to union security? Nowhere have I been able to find any clear-cut declaration from any official in Ontario as to whether or not it supports the principle of union security. Therefore, throughout the country no one knows where the Ontario government stands, whether it is behind the workers who are seeking the freedom of security or whether it is behind the men who are apparently seeking to destroy that security and break the strike.
This matter should be cleared up at the earliest possible moment, and I warn the people responsible, both in Ottawa and in Toronto, that they are playing with something a little worse than fire. They are playing with fire over dynamite. If this thing once gets going out of control they will be the people who will suffer least, because there will be hundreds of thousands of people in this country, who have no chance at all to play any part directly or indirectly in dealing with the question, who will be the luckless and innocent sufferers.
Ford Motor Plant Strike .

I think we have a right to a clear-cut declaration on the part of each of these governments, and after the declaration is made, then the next thing would be to pass legislation. At the' present time- we must assume that both the federal government and the Ontario government favour union security. If they do, let them pass legislation at once implementing the principles of union security. If they favour only partial union security, let them pass legislation that will go as far as they support it. Then everyone will know where they stand. If it should be that the federal government and the provincial government , pass legislation, even by order in council, clearly implementing the principles of union security, then immediately we should be able to proceed in settling the strike.
Mr. Campbell, 1 believe, has definitely declared, in the statement read this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina, that if the governments in Canada would pass legislation implementing union security, the plant would fall in line. Can a man do more than that? After all, why should Mr. Campbell have to take the responsibility for passing legislation in the Dominion of Canada to deal with industrial disputes? Surely, if the governments in Canada have any back-bone and leadership at all they are qualified to pass that legislation and will do so.
The matter could be taken care of very easily by order in council by each of the governments-order in council subject to ratification by the legislatures concerned. They could deal with the whole matter as an emergency situation. If, after the statement made by Mr. Campbell that the Ford Motor company would fall into line with legislation passed by those Iiaving authority, the company hesitated or delayed in keeping its promise implied by that statement of Mr. Campbell, then the Ontario government should appoint a provincial commissioner with full authority, power and responsibility to act in order to effect a settlement. That is the constitutional step.
There are too many people in this country who are talking about having the central government assume power. Mr. Dupiessis, in the statement read this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina, indicated definitely that he does not propose to surrender provincial rights, and there is certainly no reason why he should. There is a right way to go about these matters. Let the Ontario government take the lead by appointing a commissioner, and then let the federal government, acting through its Department of Labour, appoint, a similar commissioner with power to cooperate with the provincial commissioner and with the full authority of this parliament behind him.

This is the procedure to follow and it should not be any longer delayed. The members of the Social Credit 'movement favour having both the provincial and the federal government pass legislation implementing the principle of union security. This will involve everything, practically, as far as I know, that the strikers in Windsor have asked for. They call it union security and we take their term.
The hon. member for Spadina pointed out that no such legislation as I have indicated is on the statute books of the United States. That may be, but Alberta already has legislation implementing the principles of union security and certainly if Alberta can pass such legislation, so can Ontario. I understand that Saskatchewan has similar legislation.
What are the steps that ought to be taken immediately? If it is a fact that Mr. Blackwell, attorney general of Ontario, has acknowledged that the federal government has the authority to deal with this dispute under the War Measures Act, and if it is a fact that he has thereby virtually implied that he is willing that the federal government should use that authority in the case of this dispute, then the Ontario government has in effect invited the federal government to act. If the Minister of Labour will make sure that this was the intention behind the statement made by Mr. Blackwell, thereby obtaining the full consent and permission of Ontario to deal with this problem, then he will have a clear way before him, and he should have an order in council passed immediately by the cabinet of this parliament implementing the policy of union security. Then he should appoint a commissioner with full power and responsibility to act. He should give that commissioner instructions to go to Windsor and settle this dispute without further delay.

For the information of the hon. member may I say that, in Ontario, municipal councils have no jurisdiction over police forces. The administration of law and order in a local community is vested, not in the municipal council, but in the local police commission. The initial responsibility in Windsor rests with the police commission of that city. They are the only body with power to direct the movements of the local,police. The city council has no such power.
TMr. Fleming.]
The request for police assistance which went to the attorney general was a request from the police commission of Windsor, the proper body to make such a request. All the attorney general did was to comply with the request made by the body authorized to make it. When we hear suggestions that the -attorney general should have disregarded that request from the police commission at Windsor, and instead should have acted upon the request from the mayor, such suggestions entirely overlook the proper constitutional relationship, on the one hand of the police commission and on the other hand of the municipal council.

The people of Canada are not at war with the Ford strikers; they are with them in their desire to achieve some measure of the industrial democracy and better standard of living which they believe this war was fought for. Therefore, I plead with the Acting Prime Minister to consider seriously whether he and his government have not made a mistake in permitting the police to go to Windsor and to consider seriously withdrawing the police from that city to-night. I address my plea not only to the Acting Prime Minister but to every minister of the government, for all of them are showing how deeply they appreciate the situation by their presence here throughout this debate. I address my appeal particularly to the Secretary of State because of the interest he must very naturally take in this situation, obtaining as it does in vis own city.
There was a day not so very long ago when very simple measures would have settled the strike. We made such proposals from time to time from this part of the house and have had some support from some other quarters. But the situation has been allowed to drift, and inflammatory action has been taken that has made it worse, so that now it cannot be settled by one simple stroke. What I want to say now is this, withdrawing the police will obviate undesirable consequences, but that in itself will not be sufficient to settle the strike. A further step will have, to be taken, but I emphasize that withdrawal of the police is the first step.
Alter that is done, I suggest to the Acting Prime Minister and to the other members of the government that there is a further step which must be taken if the dispute itself between the Ford Motor company and its employees is to be settled. It has been said a number of times to-day that- the first thing to do is to put a government controller in, take over the plant and start it functioning once again. But even that does not go io the root of the matter. The root of the matter is the whole question of union security; and if the government really wants not only to obviate undesirable consequences by with' drawing the police but to settle the dispute itself, its other step is to convene a meeting

of the cabinet council and to pass an order in council amending P.C. 1003 to provide for union security as a provision in collective agreements when such security is desired by the union which is properly certified according to the order in council.
This request, the plea that provision be made for union security, has not only come from some of us in this house but has been made repeatedly to 'the government directly by the representatives of organized labour. I remind 'the government specifically that last spring when the Canadian Congress of Labour met with a committee of the cabinet to lay before 'the government its recommendations, one of them had to do with union security. Let me read to the government the actual terms of that recommendation:
We therefore recommend to the council that it should urge that suitable provision be introduced in the regulations-
The reference is to the regulations under P.C. 1003.
-to give authority to the labour relations board in much the same way as now provided frn grievance procedure, to decide and establish in any specific case, that the collective agreement negotiated or to be negotiated, is to include, or be deemed to include, such provision in relation to union security whether for union shop, maintenance of membership and/or deduction for union dues, as the board decides is proper. Failure to comply with any such order or direction of the board should constitute an unfair labour practice. It should also be provided that the board shall have no authority to order any provisions of union security inferior to those prevailing in the existing agreement or in any agreement which expired automatically before the application.
I have given that quotation for various reasons; first, to make it clear that what we . are asking for is not merely some idea that we have cooked up. It is the specific request of organized labour, which organized labour has made to the government. I have also read it to show that organized labour has thought the matter through and has made a specific suggestion which fits into the labour machinery now in effect in this country, namely, P.C. 1003.
I go on and remind the government that that request for an amendment to P.C. 1003 has been made not only by the Canadian Congress of Labour but by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. I hold in my hand a copy of the memorandum presented to the dominion government by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on Monday, April 23, 1945. One paragraph of their memorandum, dealing with P.C. 1003, reads as follows:
