speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No, and I am glad the minister has asked that question, and I may say further that even the Saskatchewan legislation of which we are boasting so much-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Just a minute; treat this thing with a little seriousness. Even that Saskatchewan legislation does not include a compulsory provision so far as union shop is concerned. The Saskatchewan act compels maintenance of membership. But under this
kind of legislation in the United States the rights of employees have been sufficiently protected through other sections that define unfair labour practices, and unions have gained sufficient strength, so that it has become, shall I say, impossible for a company like Ford over there to practice against employees the things which that company did in Canada; and it was on the basis of that greater union strength, achieved through legislative protection, that they voluntarily agreed to the union shop which the employees there were asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is on a voluntary basis there, though.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: With respect to the checkoff and a union shop along the lines as defined this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina, that is not required by the Wagner act. What it does is one step less, but it so protects employees against unfair practices of employers and thus strengthens the position of the unions, so that there is .no point to employers trying to break up the organization. That is basically what you have in .the situation at Windsor, as the government knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Oh, well-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The Ford company in
Canada has used every loophole there was in the legislation to seek the disintegration of the union. The union in the United States in its organization is thoroughly protected by the terms of the Wagner act, and that protection gives it a strength which has enabled it to bargain on a much more equal basis than you can ever bargain on under the terms of the legislation which is contained in P.C. 1003. I point out to the minister that any requests made in the proposals of the Canadian Congress of Labour and the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada do not go to the extent of the compulsion he asked me about a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is my point. The hon. gentleman is going to that length when he is asking us to pass an order in council to-night compelling the insertion of a clause providing for so-called union security if this union wants it in' this dispute and if any union wants it in any dispute. He is asking that there be an order in council compelling the insertion of that clause in the agreement between employer and employee, and I am asking him if that is not going much farther than has been gone in any legislation anywhere.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It goes farther than the legislation in the United States; and the United States legislation goes farther than the legislation in England. And yet the practice in England is more advanced than it is in
1S40
Ford Motor Plant.Strike

the United States. What you have to deal with is the situation as it exists. Our situation in Canada requires more advanced legislation to achieve even as much as they have in the United States, let alone England.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Why? Because our governments have allowed labour relations to drift into the kind of situation that confronts us to-night at Windsor.
Perhaps there is not much more I should . say at this point, because if I talk much longer I may do the kind of thing I do not want to do; that is, to start making comparisons and throwing political footballs around. What I am mainly concerned with is that the government, consider the risks involved in letting the situation stand as it is in Windsor to-night, consider withdrawing the police, and go on to take the further step of passing the necessary order in council which will provide for union security, so that the dispute at Windsor can be properly settled vithojit any further delay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Will the hon. member state that all the fault lies with the company?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I suppose there have been human errors on the part of some of the men, but the basic fault underlying the situation at Windsor lies definitely with the company, and in the main lies with one man, Wallace Campbell. True as that is, it is water under the bridge. To-night we have a dangerous situation. Without saying that anyone is necessarily responsible for what has brought about the situation, I suggest that this government is responsible for taking the steps to solve the problem as it now stands.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
To-night we have the second
debate on the Ford strike. That is all to the good, because we have the responsibility of deciding what will be the pattern of post-war labour relations. Will it be police, or will it be legislation? What the great majority of the people want is legislation.
Our first debate took place a few days before the conference in Toronto, the conference which was attended by the Minister of Labour, representatives from the union and from the company. That conference failed, because the minister did not come to the conference prepared to offer a solution of the problem. Conferences are all very well; they never do any harm; but there must also be concrete proposals, and the proposals which were made by the Minister of Labour offered less than what was proposed by Mr. Justice Richards before the strike. It was obvious that the workers, who have been out on strike for quite a few
FMr. Knowles. 1
weeks, were not going to accept less than what they were offered before the strike. Mr. Campbell would not even listen to those proposals. He told some people outside the conference that he would starve the workers into submission, and he has quite a bit of money to do it with-millions upon millions of reserve funds.
After the conference broke up, nothing happened. This government failed to give a lead; they failed to take the next step. There was one proposal for an arbitrator. But, as has already been explained by one member to-day, it was very hard for workers out on strike for about seven weeks to say, "All right, we will go back to work now and see what is going to happen," and this after seventeen months of boards and hearings. The workers wanted something more substantial than merely a word from the minister to go back; the company did not reply for quite a while; and when it did reply, as we were told to-day. it rejected the proposal for an arbitrator. The result of the government's inactivity is the extension of the strike.
Who is to blame? The workers have been quite reasonable. When the proposal for an arbitrator came down they called a meeting. All the strikers came together and the proposal was put before them. They rejected it. I understand, however, they came back with additional proposals that would have led to some understanding, but the employer merely said, "We will have nothing to do with any of your proposals." Again I ask, who is to blame? Campbell and no one else.
After that failed, then came the police, and I assure hon. members that the coming of police into a city, their presence in that city, is an interference on behalf of the employer, no matter what reason they may offer. That is the way the workers feel about it, and generally the presence of police aggravates a strike situation. I have been in such situations. It creates an altogether new situation and anything is liable to happen. Paid pro-vocators have been known in the past to bring about the calling of police into a strike. Paid provocators have been known in the past to lead to bloodshed and all sorts of consequences in order to break a strike. Paid provocators have been known to organized workers for years. Books and pamphlets have been written on the subject.	,
The police have never settled a strike. What can settle a strike and what must settle the strike is government intervention. I am not interested in any political football. I am not interested in knowing who was responsible for the police going in. The responsibility is

Ford Motor Plant Strike
provincial and federal. They are both responsible. Instead, they should be working together to settle the strike. I have before me a report of the meeting that took place in Toronto at that conference about which I spoke earlier. At that conference Mr. Blackwell said that he was quite willing to cooperate with the federal government in amending order in council 1003. At that conference, too, Mr. Campbell said that., if the federal government thought union security was a good thing they should put it on the statute books and he would be willing to go along. That was a basis for settling the strike.
A few weeks ago I asked two questions of the minister as to what had happened at the conference, and I suggested that Messrs. Blackwell and Campbell made such proposals. He told me I had the wrong pipeline. I think we should get more serious replies from our ministers when we ask questions, because we want to find out what is happening in these matters.
Do we need compulsory ' legislation for union security? I say that we do. Why? Because in Canada-I do not know what it is like elsewhere-we have people of the type of Campbell. That is why it is necessary. If we had more enlightened employers who would go in for collective security without compulsory legislation it would be fine, but seemingly we need it over here; and if we need it, it is not necessary for us to base our actions on what is done in any other country. We live in Canada, ours is a different sort of country, and our legislation should be based upon Canadian needs and not on those of the United States or anywhere else.
The sending in of the police has served only one purpose, to encourage the Ford company and nothing else. The sending in of police, no matter what any hon. member says, means that the government has allied itself with the employers. That is what it means to the workers. That is what the people in Montreal feel. I was in Montreal over the week-end, and the workers there are greatly disturbed over wrhat is happening in Windsor.
Last week the organized workers in Montreal contributed nearly five thousand dollars toward the Ford strikers, an excellent example of unity between the English and the French-Canadian people in Canada. At a meeting in my constituency nearly $1,100 was contributed to the Ford strike.
That is the way the people feel, and unless Mr. Blackwell and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) or rather the Minister of Labour and Mr. Drew, find a quick solution
we are going to have strikes throughout the country. And no one will have to organize them. They will come because the people feel insecure and do not like this police pattern at the present time. That is not what our. boys fought for. The workers will not take police- rule lying down.
There are now 700,000 organized workers in Canada. This is not the Canada of 1919, 1920, and 1921 or of the crisis years. We have hundreds of thousands of young men who fought and theirs is a different sort of determination. They will not stand for intimidation by the police. They want initiative shown by this government and the creation of a different pattern for labour-employer relations.
To-day a conference opened in Washington addressed by President Truman. It was a conference on management and labour. The conference was composed of representatives from the chamber of commerce, the manufacturers' association and a number of big firms in the United States and leaders of trade unions. The United States Minister of Labour, Mr. Schwellenbach, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Wallace, represented the government. They are trying to work out a pattern for peace in industry in the United States. Can this government say that we have done the same thing in Canada? Can this government say that we have tried the same thing in Canada? No. In preparation for this conference Mr. Truman spoke last week to a number of labour leaders to pave the way for a peaceful solution. A few days earlier he announced that it would now be possible to increase sub-standard wages. That is a much bolder way of meeting the situation than we have in Canada at the present time. We need similar action. The type of action we need to-day is (1) union security. That is what the workers want as a minimum. (2) The right of workers to bargain on wages that are below fifty cents; (3) immediate withdrawal of the police, and a rapid settlement of the strike with the government appointing a controller. If we do that we shall be creating much better post-war industrial relations than we are creating at the present time with the police. The police will not solve anything; we need legislation. This government has the power to act. I do not care whether it is the provincial government or the federal government; let them come to an understanding and they can give us that legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am sure that every member of this committee will appreciate that if there is anyone who has a right and a duty to say something on this matter it is myself, not only because I am a member of the
Ford Motor Plant Strike

government, blit because I represent one of the constituencies where the scene of the circumstances under discussion exists.
I had urged upon my good friend, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who I think perhaps would agree without any reservation that no one in this house has at heart to any greater extent than I have the cause and the welfare of labour, that it might be advisable, in view of the actual situation and of the dispatch to Windsor to-day of the Minister of Labour, that whatever we say here to-day be tempered with the utmost of responsibility. I do not quarrel, however, with his taking the position that in his judgment the matter should be discussed. Since the matter has been discussed, I have been the recipient of telephone calls and almost extraordinary number of telegrams, which causes me to 'believe that if every member of this committee were- aware of the nature of some of them, and the source of them-and their source is not by any means entirely in the employer group-they would appreciate that what we must not forget at this moment, above all else, is that the man on whose shoulders rests the immediate responsibility as Minister of Labour of the Dominion of Canada has left this chamber to go to Windsor. That circumstance must not be *forgotten in the discussion before this committee.
I do not propose to say anything that is going to add to the difficulty of his task, and to the tremendous and important consequences of it. What the result will be I do not know, but I do know this; having come from AVindsor only over the week-end, and having conferred with all sorts of people, I do know how the people of my city feel. And if I rise in my place to-night in this forum of the nation it is largely to say things that will perhaps serve to place upon the judgment of the people whom I represent in this house the right kind of temper so that they will not be misjudged.
The people of Windsor are law-abiding, as good citizens as one will find in any community of this country. They are people who, when the situation is placed before them in proper perspective, will have as deep a respect for the agencies of authority and of law as any other community in Canada. But I would not be doing my duty if I did not say first of all that no one yet, largely because they do not live in the community, has touched upon, except the member for Spadina in some particulars, the provocations and the historical situations that have led to the present difficulty. I have said that my constituents are a law-abiding people; they are. They belong to a union community. That does not make them less lawful or less respectful of the agencies of authority; but the vast majority
PMr. Martin.]
of them work in an industry whose labour relations policy I could not refrain from saying has not been an enlightened one over the years. They work in an industry where men do not live in that kind of city can have no full appreciation of the social consequences, an industry where it is said they are well paid-well paid by the day. But, as I said here a month ago, when one analyses the annual wage output, it is wholly inadequate, as every person in that community knows. During the war these men, many of whom have served overseas and have come back to work in that plant, many of them the fathers of men who have served in the armed forces, and some of whom have died, have worked during the war doing important war work on an efficient basis.
In reviewing Canada's war effort in terms of war production not so long ago, the Minister of Munitions and Supply said in this house that the contribution of the automobile industry in Canada in terms of the production of vehicles was one of the epics on the home front of this country. In saying that, he was thereby saying that the men who worked on the assembly line, in the foundry of that plant and of other plants of that kind, had done a great job during the war. The reason I mention that is that when tempers are hot. when the emotions of the people are stirred, they are apt to pass judgment on a community when they are not fully aware of all the implications.
This government-and I say this to the hon. member for Vancouver East with all the sincerity that I iiave-has not set out on a policy of depressing wages. I ask him to believe that.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I will believe that when you bring in the evidence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
All right; I am prepared to deal with that. I ask the hon. member, does he honestly think that anyone would deliberately set out on a policy of depressing wages? I can tell him that with regard to this particular industry the plans of this administration are altogether otherwise, as I shall endeavour to show. But what I wish to point out is this-and it has to be said, in view of what the hon. member for Spadina said to-day-as I suggested earlier, and not without reason, there were some sections of industry who by their own professions, some of whom have since criticized what I have said in the house, have written to me beforehand clearly indicating their intentions with regard to trade union integrity and union existence.
This much must be borne in mind: You cannot, by any act of anyone destroy the existence of trade union organizations in this

Ford Motor Plant Strike
or any other country. Those institutions are .here to stay, and I think they are a good (hing to have stay here. I think we should be satisfied with our labour leaders, on the whole. The heads of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the heads of the Canadian Congress of Labour and of all the other national organizations are well intentioned men who have no other purpose than that of furthering the interests of the workers along responsible lines.
What I have said about them I say about many of the trade union leaders and trade union men in my own community. Who are these men who, because of the temper of this particular circumstance, will be misjudged? They are just ordinary men and women. One of my own family who has lived in this country for generations, working in that plant, was firmly convinced of the power and desirability of trade union movements. That for the most part represents the character of the people in this particular trade union organization.
I do not say that there are not at work influences which maliciously will use some of these people. But I do not think that to say more than that at this time under the circumstances will help. But when I do say it, the hon. member for Cape Breton South will know what I have reference to.
In this dispute I would not be fair to myself if I did not say here-and this is the first chance I have had really to say it-that I have not sat by as one of the members for that district, nor has my colleague the hon. member for Essex West sat by, and done nothing. I would not be true if I did not say that there has not been a night when, through this fantastic experience, I have not been greatly concerned about it. Perhaps I knew more about what was happening than many did.
I wish to say that at the time this dispute broke out, almost from the very hour I was in conference in this city with the Minister of Labour, and with one of the leading men in the organization, trying to head off a situation which seemed to be almost inevitable. From that moment on, there has not been a day, there has not been an hour since I have been in the house that in some way or another tliis matter has not received my full attention. I say that because to-night, when there are thousands of men and women who perhaps sometimes have no conception of what is involved, or what it is all about, I want them to know-and I have a right to say this-that when I made professions to them at various times as a public man I meant everything I said, that I have not forgotten
their situation and their problem at this time, nor did I forget it in the last few months. I think hon. members in all parts of the house will believe me when I say-whether it has been adequate enough or not-that I have done everything that I could possibly do to try to resolve this matter in a manner which would be just to the parties concerned, in a manner which would see that the integrity of the trade union moyement in that particular community was maintained, and to see that they are returned to work under the most favourable circumstances.
If at this time it appears that thus far we have not succeeded, it is not because there has not been an effort or because there has been a betrayal of convictions. The situation is a difficult one.
Speaking on behalf of the government, the Acting Prime Minister said that there would be no effort-and if there was I Could not support it-by compulsion on the part of police powers to break the strike. That is elementary. He has stated that, and that is the situation.
What has happened since three o'clock, I do not know. But I do know that the municipal government of the city of Windsor to-day, meeting as we are, and as deeply concerned about the whole situation, did urge upon both parties that an independent opportunity be given to determine the nature of any situation in connection with the power plant, without the operation of which in the event of settlement of the dispute there can be no return to work.
What that investigation will show, I do not know. But I understand from the latest information I have had that that proposal is under way. I do not know the full particulars; they have not yet come to me. When that does come about, I have not a"ny doubt that if the situation is placed properly before the men, as to what they are doing, the result will be satisfactory. But this situation must be placed before them. The Minister of Finance to-day, in rising in his place and explaining the insurance situation, was not actuated by any desire to preserve proprietary interests also. And I say this, that the country knows that, because of the kind of man he is primarily. The Minister of Finance is not capable of having any other interests than the welfare of the people of this country at heart; for in bringing out the picture from the underwriters' point of view he had only one concern, and that was to see that when this dispute is settled-and, please God let it be settled quickly-it will be settled in such a way that the men can return to their work with a minimum of lost time.
Strike at Ford Mdtor Plant

Ford Motor Plant Strike
Although there have been provocations,.and particularly to-night, I do not want to say [DOT] anything by way of criticism of what has been said. But I do feel that what the Minister of Finance said to-day in this connection did not justify the comment that was made about it.
We cannot touch the basic issues here tonight. The Minister of Labour has gone to Windsor. I have been in touch with him within the last hour or hour and a half. In the light of what I know he is attempting -whether he will succeed or not I do not know-
I do not propose to say anything by way of final suggestion until I know that his efforts have been exhausted. And that is what I respectfully suggest, with all the force and sincerity I can muster, should be the situation.
But I can say this, that employers in that area well know that at the basis of this problem is not the metaphysical debate that has taken place here to-day and this evening about certain modes of settling disputes. Basic in this problem is what Mr. Attlee said the other day with regard to the dockworkers -no formula will succeed in industrial or in any other relations unless there is good faith on all sides. There has not been good faith on -all sides. The Minister of Labour has sent into this particular plant-I hesitate to say a word of complaint about my own community, which is at the moment perhaps the most troublesome in industrial relations in the country-no less than three different boards headed by three different men who were disposed toward trying to bring about a solution that was in the interests of both parties. The conduct on some occasions, for instance toward Mr. Justice Richards, not by the men but by certain of the employers in that plant, indicated-that there was an inadequate expression of good faith.
Mr. Burt, the regional director of the UAW-CIO-whatever may be said about him and I know lots of things will be said about him;
I have been in contact with him now for two months not without a day passing, at times not without two or three hours passing

has made every effort, fighting loyally for his men, to try to effect an amicable settlement. He said, "If we once get this problem on a basis where we can sit down across the table as men without hate engendering on both sides; if we can accomplish that, then we shall have solved the basic difficulty of this dispute."
That is what we have to try to do. These other matters involving jurisdiction between provinces and the dominion are important over a long period, but basic in it is the recognition on the part of the employer and on the part
[Mr. MartinJ
of the worker that each has a responsibility as well as an Obligation, and that if each approaches the problem in the same spirit of understanding and cooperation, the problem can be solved. That does not exist. Since we are meeting ijor the moment to deal with the current situation, not as to what the ultimate law shall be-on these things I have elsewhere expressed myself-in terms of the immediate problem that faces this county to-night, I think the first thing we must do is to impress on both sides the necessity, despite the suspicions and hate and enmity that exist, of sitting down at the earliest possible moment to deal with one another, each with rights, each with privileges and each with obligations.
That may to some seem simply parabolic. It will be said that all I have done is to preach. If I have done nothing else, I hope I have done that much, for, in the words of Mr. Attlee, who said only on Friday last, there is a stage in government when no matter what the differences be, whether they be between nations or whether they be between peoples in a country; no matter what may be the solution for the problems of a nation, unless there is understanding these cannot even be approached. That is the issue which I think faces us.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply has tried to deal with these. Some will say by way of criticism that it was not done effectively, but there are explanations. Last May in this very building I sat in at a conference between the united automobile workers, the Minister of Munitions and Supply and some of his officials, when there was a full disclosure of the reconversion situation which existed at that time. I think that was a model conference. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, who is abused so often without any justification because his point of view is not always fully understood or appreciated, said, "What I want to try to do is to establish in this industry and in other industries as close a thing as I can to democracy in industry and government; I want to get on a firm basis whereby the employers and workers, sitting in with government on a friendly basis can discuss, not only the rights of labour but the rights and the obligations and the difficulties of industry, to let labour see these so that they can share in and know them."	.
Here comes the industrial council idea, which first came to this country from his lips. It may not have succeeded. We have not gone as far with it as one would like, but I say there are reasons. You cannot force those things down anyone's throat. It is all very well to say you can do this, but you cannot force men to understand, one another. It is regrettable

Ford Motor Plant Strike
that in this particular industry it has not been possible to do that, but that is no reason why it should not be attempted.
The hon. member for Spadina, speaking in this house a month ago, said that there may have to be changed faces. Whatever that means, I do not think there is much point in my explaining it at this moment. Let us hope, if that does take place, that there will be a complete reorientation. These things are done. I think all of us in this country, without trying to pause for the purposes of political advantage, can perhaps make suggestions. All of us are interested in labour; all of us are trying to get a solution of this problem. We can as a government, we can as a parliament take those general steps by which understanding between labour and management may be pursued.
Viewing the. "situation in my own city tonight, and disturbed by the news from all sides, I say that I have no doubt that the vast majority of the men and women in that community do not want disorder. I have every belief that if there can be, as I hope there will be, a maintenance of cool-headedness, and a recognition on the part of all that this government has always recognized the rights of labour to organize and has taken steps to maintain the gains and strength of labour, this problem going through its difficult stage will not go without solution.
I can only say, speaking in my capacity as the member for Essex East, that I sincere!}' hope that God's help will go to those who at this moment-the Minister of Labour from this government and others-are working for a satisfactory solution of this problem, one that will not result in the destruction of the union but will result in its continued existence on a basis of cooperation and a basis of rational and civilized relationship with the employer. Can I say anything else at this stage that will help or that will prove where my convictions lie?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We have had quite a lengthy discussion on this serious problem, and I was wondering if hon. members of the committee would be ready to proceed with the estimates we have before us?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I know that everyone in the house has listened with close attention to the moving speech that has just been made by the Secretary of State. I do not think there is any member who would doubt his sincere concern over this very difficult situation. After the months of work and thought and effort that he must have devoted to endeavours to settle this dispute, I am sure
that every member of the house will have every sympathy for him. But it needs to be said at the conclusion of his very moving speech that he has offered no solution of the Ford strike. I go farther and say that the government has not offered us any solution of the Ford strike. This debate has been going on since about four o'clock this afternoon, and no one can blame you, Mr. Chairman, for having suggested that it might now come to an end because, although this concerns a matter of the very gravest importance to Canada and affects every part of our country, not only the city of Windsor but all Canada, I do not think I have ever listened to a debate so inconclusive since I entered the house.
What have we had? From the speakers to my left of the C.C.F. party who raised this question it was not until after the dinner interval that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre got down to the question of union security.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is not correct. I mentioned it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Hon. members of the C.C.F. to my left have said1 first of all that they are against law and' order being upheld by the police going in, and they want the police removed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I must take exception to that and ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has the floor and I know that if he has offended any member he will withdraw his statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR

If the hon. member for Vancouver East is offended by my remarks I state that I mean no offense to him whatever. I was saying that the hon. member and his colleagues have said that the police should be withdrawn from Windsor, and I state that in making that request they are not upholding law and order. That is one thing they have suggested.
The next thing they suggested was a controller, and the hon. member for Cape Breton South in the course of his remarks said that if a controller were appointed he thought the parties to the dispute could be got around the conference table. If that really is the case; if on the appointment of a controller the Ford Company and the union could sit around the conference table and come to an agreement on the issue of union security, then I for one would be in favour of the appointment of a controller to-night.

But there is more than that. We have had from the hon. member for Vancouver East the suggestion that union security or the compulsory union shop should be passed in the form of an order in council to-night. I suggest that the hon. members of the C.C.F. party who have spoken in this debate have first of all shown that they were indifferent as to whether illegal action was carried on-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman says that we are indifferent as to whether things should be done legally or not. That is completely untrue and should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, in my opinion it is a legitimate argument. I do not wish to cause any offence to my hon. friends to the left. I was simply drawing an inference which I thought was a fair one from their arguments, and if they will allow me to state my case I think they will find that they do not come off too badly.
The point I wished to make when I was, in my view, Mr. Chairman, very rudely interrupted, was simply that the C.C.F. members who have raised this question have spoken on it as inconclusively as have the government, have shown an indifference to the real issue, and have suggested to the government

no solution of the dispute which could possibly be accepted in this country. The reason why hon. members to the left will never be able to form a government in this country is that they are so far to the left that they will seize one side of a case and press it before this house as if the interests and rights and the duties of the other party to a dispute such as this were of no concern at all.
The C.C.F. members have suggested, first of all, that a controller be appointed, and, second, that P.C. 1003 be amended by writing into the statute book a law compelling all Canadians to join a union without any safeguard of the rights of the individual so forced to join a union. They simply call for a compulsory union shop for every worker, and- * again I use this_ word because I can think of no other-they seem to be indifferent whether that worker whom they would force to join a union wishes to abide by all the rules and objects of the union. They do not offer him any protection once he so joins. That is my objection to the argument advanced by the C.C.F. Let me repeat, however, that, if I really believed that this strike could be settled in the way that the hon. member for Cape Breton South has suggested, by the appointment of a controller and the bringing about of a private agreement between the two parties, I would be entirely behind his suggestion. But it is not my belief that this issue of union security can be settled by private parties around a conference table.
Some weeks ago I went to Windsor and there saw all the parties to the dispute-the company, the union, the men on the picket lines, and private citizens in Windsor, and talked to many people. I was there for only twelve hours, and1 therefore the impressions I gained must be judged in the light of that short visit. But I did gain some vividi impressions which I wish to express to the committee this evening. I can do so best in one short sentence; I came to the conclusion that the company was wrong, that the union was wrong, and that the men were right.
I will elaborate that a little. I say that the company was wrong for the same reason that the Secretary of State said so, and that is, this question of the low annual wage. Over a long period of years that has been the sore which has festered in the workers in that company. After all, over a long period of years the management of that company has failed to satisfy its workers so that they worked in harmony with the management. For that reason I say that the company was wrong.

Ford Motor Plant Strike
Then I say that the union was wrong; and here, perhaps, is where my hon. friends on my left and I get at loggerheads. I say that the union is clearly wrong, no matter what the provocation, when it breaks the law of this land, and it broke the law when it engaged in other than peaceful picketing. When once a citizen breaks the law the proper authority has no recourse but to step in and uphold the law, and that is what the government of Ontario has done.
I do not blame a great deal either the company or the union; it always happens in strikes that there is some excess on one side or the other. I said that the men are right. All they really want is, not the union security which is now demanded, but a reasonable annual wage, and surely they are entitled to that and ought to get it. They want, of course, the right to negotiate on a fair basis in order to obtain that reasonable annual wage and fair working conditions, and that is why this issue of union security is before the committee now, because the union believes and the workers believe that, without what they term union security, they cannot bargain on equal terms with management.
The other impression I got when I was at Windsor was that there was bad blood between the parties. We all know that. It has been caused by years of strife instead of years of cooperation, and particularly by recent incidents,- such as the pulling out of the power plant workers which annoyed the company terrifically, and continual indecision and delay over bargaining, which lasted for eighteen months and annoyed the union considerably. The result is that it has come down to a trial of strength, and both parties are thinking more of the most recent incident which arouses their ire against the other than of the fundamental issues. For that reason a settlement between the parties is made very difficult.
But there is another party to this argument and this trouble which has not come into this discussion as often as it should. That other body is this parliament. This parliament has left this nettle to be grasped by a private business	concern-the	company-and the
union. We of this parliament have not grasped it ourselves. I am speaking to-night because I think that until this parliament grasps the nettle, faces up to the issue of union security, and decides whether union security is good for the people of Canada or bad for them, this problem will never be settled in this country and it will bedevil our industrial 47696-117
relations and the whole process of reconversion from war to peace, no matter what may happen to the present Ford strike.
The parties to this dispute have no common ground. In my view there is no midway point between union security and no union security. Other matters are involved, such as maintenance of membership and the voluntary or compulsory check-off wdthout maintenance of membership; but these are comparatively nebulous things; when you get right down to business it is union security or no union security which is the root of the problem.
I wish to review for a moment the state of this matter as it affects parliament. I was surprised-and I do not want to have another rough and tumble with hon. members on my left-

I will, indeed. I was just coming to that.
Much has been said about the constitutional issue involved in this problem. It is said that this is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. I would merely point out that under the War Measures Act this parliament has the power to deal with this issue. Even if the government had no such power under the War Measures Act, which of course they have, in a few days they are going to introduce an emergency powers bill, which, if passed in its present form, will put beyond peradventure of doubt the question of where the power lies. And I say to the committee that where the power lies, there lies the responsibility. This, therefore, is not a matter for the provincial government. I want, however, to say this, that there are many of us, as hon. members opposite well know, who do not agree that the present federal government should have the great powers which they are claiming in that bill. But our disagreement would be that

Ford Motor Plant Strike

much stronger, that much more forceful were we to learn that they were going to take these powers and then refrain from exercising them and prevent the provincial government from exercising them.
So that this matter lies squarely at the door of this government. Further, I say that it lies squarely at the door of this parliament. The present legislation with regard to these disputes goes as far as compulsory collective bargaining and conciliation procedure, and that compulsory collective bargaining and conciliation procedure, under P.C. 1003, is very good legislation and handles these two particular matters very well. But the difficulty we are up against is that, once collective bargaining and conciliation procedures stop, the law of the jungle takes their place in industrial relations. There is no law governing this Ford strike dispute, and therefore it comes down to a straight trial of strength between the two parties.
This is a dispute of personalities, of principles and of ideologies. It is not a bargaining on wages or hours of work or anything like that. There are fundamental principles involved in it and they are not suited to be settled between private parties. They are not suited to be settled on the basis of who is the stronger. They are suited to be settled only by the calm deliberation of an assembly such as this. That is the great point I want to make in this house. In other words, they must be settled by legislation.
I say that these strikes on union security must not be allowed to rend this country any more, and if they do so the responsibility lies upon us in this chamber-and I do not leave it only on hon. gentlemen opposite; I include all of us. Canada does not want these strikes on the issue of union security any more; Canada cannot afford to have them any more. We have a duty not only to the Ford company, not only to the Ford workers, not only to the Ford union, but to the general public of this country, the producers and consumers and those engaged in secondary industry, all of whom are immediately and personally affected by strikes such as this and by issues such as the one before us.
Canada wants peace, industrial and internal as well as international, and she wants full employment. We cannot have full employment unless we maintain the purchasing power of this country; and every industrial dispute, no matter how caused or whatever else it may do, affects the purchasing power of the country and endangers our chance of full employment.
I wish to deal more closely with the question of union security. I am in favour of strong

trades unions, very strong trades unions; and when I say strong trades unions I mean trades unions which are strong enough to sit down and bargain on equal terms with employers. When you are sitting down and bargaining on equal terms with a great limited company you have to be pretty strong, and I would remind hon. members of what the hon. member for Calgary West said in the house some time ago: What is the good of talking about collective bargaining on a fair basis if one party is sitting down without any money and the other party is sitting down with all the money? That is what I mean by strong trades unions.
I believe that in order that trades unions may grow to equal strength with the companies they must not only be recognized by this parliament, as they are under the collective bargaining procedure; they must be more than recognized. They must be approved by this parliament, so that they can occupy an honoured and respected place in our society. Many of them do that at the present time. For instance, the railway unions are probably among our most respected and beneficial institutions. But there are many unions still in this country that are not so honoured and respected; they are objects of suspicion and mistrust. They may not earn that suspicion and mistrust; I do not say that they do. But throughout this country there are many people, perhaps not directly concerned with labour disputes, who do distrust some of these unions and are suspicious of their aims. They wonder whether those aims are really aims in favour of the workers.
I say again that I do not know the right and wrong of that; I simply state what is the case. I go farther and say that there are also in the industrial ranks, among workers in plants, men who are suspicious of or mistrust perhaps even the particular union in the plant in which they are working. That is a thing that we in this parliament must remove.
We must go sponsor for those trades unions which are worthy of our sponsorship and lift them up so that nobody can cast suspicion or mistrust upon them. That is one of the duties of this parliament. Above all else, parliament has a duty to lead in bringing about that state of affairs which the Secretary of State mentioned so properly to-night-that cooperation and spirit of mutual trust between the parties to industrial relations. It is not enough for us to sit and hope and pray that the day will come when they will sit down together as mutual friends. This parliament has a duty to lead them to that spirit of trust of which the hon. member spoke.
In making a concrete proposal on the issue of union security to-night, I am not doing so

Ford Motor Plant Strike
only because of the Ford dispute. I would hold these views as much if the Ford strike did not exist. I believe that if the Ford strike is * settled without the issue of union security being decided, we shall have another strike in another plant on another day over the same issue, and then another and1 still another until finally we are prepared' to grasp the nettle and settle the question once for all by legislation.
What I am proposing to-day is only a first step in a series of considered steps which this parliament can take in order to bring about industrial peace in this country. There are many good things ahead of us in industrial relations if we can only reach out and grasp them. There is no need for my enumerating them to the committee to-night, because in between those good things and where we stand now there are a large number of barriers. Instead of thinking of those good things ahead of us, I am going to do what I suggest has not been done in this chamber in this debate; I am going to attack directly the first great barrier, the problem of union security. What is meant by union security? We had a very good explanation of the term this afternoon from the hon. member for Spadina. So that there will be no doubt of what I mean by union security I shall give my explanation. By union security is meant, I believe, the compulsory union shop and the compulsory check-off. That is pretty blunt, and a lot of us might not like to face up to it, but I think we had better.	.
Before making my specific propostion, I wish to draw a parallel between what happened in this country in the years before the war and the present day. In the years before the war this country suffered from a series of strikes over the issue of collective bargaining, the right of a union to organize and to become the bargaining agent for the -workers in a plant. That issue iwas then known as the issue of union recognition. After a lot of strikes and a lot of trouble, that was settled on a legislative basis. We now have the right to compulsory 'collective bargaining in the statutes, and it is -working out very well indeed.
I call the attention of the committee to a significant point. We do not have any more strikes on the issue of union recognition. I say to the committee that the time has come for us to face up to the issue of union security. Let us decide fairly, after mature deliberation, one way or the other, or upon some compromise which we feel meets the issue. Let us put it on the statute books and remove from our industrial relations one more great cause of industrial conflict and strikes. As we go along in the way we have been taught to 47696-1174
follow, the way of evolution, which it is the British political genius to follow and to make to work, we shall find that one by one we are able to remove by legislation the next barrier from our path, and then the next, and finally we shall open the door to these good things which exist in industrial relation in the future. But something is required of us, and it is not very much. All that is required is that this sovereign parliament, which has the power and the duty, shall face up to its responsibility and legislate on this issue.
I wish to deal for one moment with the union shop outside of legislation. There are many union shops in this country, union shops brought about by private negotiation between the parties. To those who argue in Macleans or in any other newspaper or magazine that a union shop is undemocratic, I say that you have an undemocratic thing existing in your midst by private arrangement.

As the hon. member has
said, we have many closed shops in this country. The typographical union is a closed shop. In England there are many closed shops. There are many union shops in the United States. If we can have something by private agreement between parties which i3 undemocratic, surely it is not something we should not discuss in this house.
But there is another angle to this issue in the present strike. Here is a private employer who does not wish to grant a union shop of his own accord, and he may be quite right, because this question of bargaining between the union and the management is one of bargaining equally. If the employer thinks that if he grants the union shop the union will get too strong it is within his rights to say: "No, I cannot do that, because then I would not be bargaining equally with you. If I am stronger than you now you will be stronger than me after the agreement." Therefore it is not a thing that the company can easily give if it does not wish. Likewise it is not possible for the union to withdraw, because they do not feel that they are up to their proper strength until they have union security. Therefore it is a question of balance of power. There is only one authority which can break the deadlock, namely this sovereign parliament. It can act to enable these parties to get over this barrier, to enable them to raise themselves over the hump they have reached, so that they can go on amicably toward the future.
Ford Motor Plant Strike

I wish to make a specific proposition to the committee. I wish to suggest first of all that this government face the issue, argue it out as the two people did in Macleans, and then bring in legislation settling for all time whether or not we are to have unioh shops or upon what basis, if at all, we can have compulsory union shops in this country. If the government are not prepared to take that responsibility and to bring in their conception of what that legislation should be, I suggest that the matter be forthwith referred to the industrial relations committee of this house with instructions to proceed at once to hear evidence from all parties, not only from the parties to whom the C.C.F. listens, namely the labour unions, but to hear evidence from management; to hear evidence from the workers themselves; to hear evidence perhaps from some of the conscientious objectors to joining unions; to hear evidence from producers and) consumers and other people vitally affected by those strikes; and to hear evidence from the general public because the issue of individual freedom is inevitably bound up in this problem. Further, that the industrial relations committee be instructed to report back their recommendations, and that this parliament put on the . statute books the considered judgment of the people of Canada on this issue of union security.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as Minister of Reconstruction I think I should say a few words on this subject. The strike at Windsor is, of course, a tragedy, so far as the work of reconstruction is concerned. I think that of all the reconversion problems which have

Ford Motor Plant Strike
been studied by the department in the last eighteen months, more time and effort was put into planning the reconversion of the automobile industry than into any other, and that for the very good reason that the employees in that industry probably outnumber those of every other industry in Canada.
After a great deal of discussion with the company and with the men-because we discussed the plans with both-a plan was worked out which would have permitted the conversion of the industry with a maximum dislocation of fifteen per cent of employees for a maximum period of two months which, considering all the ramifications of the automobile industiy, with its main contractors and its parts manufacturers, would constitute a pretty fair job of reconversion.
The Ford strike has upset that plan. Not only has it upset the plan for the Ford company, but it has worked back through the parts manufacturers; and now the other main contractors are finding themselves in the same position as Ford.
I must discuss this problem with the firm conviction that nothing should be said here to-night that will add difficulty to the work which confronts the Minister of Labour in his efforts at Windsor. The Minister of Labour is a man of great experience in trade union matters, and he is, I believe, the ablest Minister, of Labour this country has seen for a good many years. He has made continued efforts to settle this dispute, and he has now gone to Windsor to put forth a last effort. I would be the last member in this house to say anything which would in any way jeopardize the work he is undertaking.
The Ford situation has been a tragedy of bad relations between management and labour. This is not the first strike in the Ford plant during the war period. We all know that one serious strike occurred lasting for a long, time. We know, too, that there have been, frequent work stoppages in that plant. We also know that in the remainder of the automobile industry there have been no labour interruptions. The same union has been operating throughout the industry. Therefore I think we must conclude that a great deal of the fault lies within the Ford plant itself. I think that the management can be very severely criticized for permitting these relations to continue. A great company such as the Ford company, one with a world-wide reputation, a company which is a great factor in the industrial life of Canada is, I think, to be severely condemned for not having created better union-management relations in its plant.
Perhaps we can say that the local of the union that controls the Ford plant has not been too well managed. I know that complaints are frequent that agreements solemnly made between union and management are not carried out. We know that there is constant friction-and usually friction is not generated from one side. Usually both sides contribute to that continued friction. It has been suggested here to-night that the cause of the friction is low wages, but I think that will hardly stand up. As a matter of fact the average wage paid in the Ford plant for the last five years is the highest that has been paid in any plant in Canada.

What have the five years
before the war to do with the situation to-night? There was in prospect no cut in wages or no cut in the take-home pay. There were a certain number of men to be laid off temporarily because of the conversion from war work to peace-time work. This would have involved a lay-off of about fifteen per cent of the personnel for a period not exceeding two months, had the conversion plan gone through smoothly. However, for the eighty-five per cent there was no loss of take-home pay, no forseeable danger that work in the plant would not be on a twelve months basis.
As a matter of fact no dispute involving wages is paramount in the discussion. The discussion that I have heard leads me to believe that the issue is so-called union security. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard defined union security as he understood it; that is, a union shop with a check-off. I may say that "union security" is a fairly recent term in the lexicon of labour disputes: I think it dates back not more than two years.
I have had some experience with labour, and I am prejudiced in favour of labour unions. I have been associated with the construction industry for a great many years. Directly and indirectly, I have dealt with labour unions over that period. The construction industry is a closed shop. If I were going back into the construction industry, I would no more think of working in that industry without always dealing with labour unions than I would think of setting out deliberately on the road to bankruptcy. The relationship between the building industry and the labour unions has been a constructive relationship. The labour unions have performed a service for the builders which the builders recognize. The builders are glad indeed to work with the labour unions. While
Ford Motor Plant Strike

Other countries have had disputes in the construction industry, Canada has been singularly free from them.
In my own work I have never had a serious dispute with organized labour, nor have t.he contractors who worked under me as engineers. I think the reason for that is that the unions were wisely led. The employers have felt that they had value from the unions for any agreement that they signed. I believe that is true union security. In discussing the present dispute, I think we had better look at real union security rather than the so-called union security which has been defined here to-night.
I had some experience with the railroads during the period I was minister in charge of the railroads in Canada. There, again, I [DOT] think you will find true union security. I think the railroad brotherhoods have more union security than almost any other labour union in Canada. Within the railroad brotherhoods there is no closed shop and there is no check-off. The railroad brotherhoods have dealt with the railroad management for a great number of years. I think tlie railroad management value the guidance of the brotherhoods just as much as the brotherhoods value their association with the management.
I have sat in on several arguments and disputes between railway labour and management, and I have been told by both sides that, once an agreement is signed, that' agreement will never be disturbed, either by labour or by management, until its full term has expired. I think that is union security of a paramount kind. Let us consider the kind of union security that has been described here to-night. We have been told that we should pass a law immediately stating that the policy of this country in labour matters will be the union shop and the check-off. We are told that we should either make it a law-

Let us discuss the situation for a moment. I was interested in the dockers' strike in the United Kingdom. There we had a newly elected Labour government, made up of men wise in labour leadership. I
["Mr. How?.]
think if we had been looking for the best people to council us as to the proper relations between labour and government we would have looked to some of the men who form the government of the United Kingdom to-day. The dockers' strike was a serious one, a good many more men being involved than are involved in the Ford dispute. The stoppage of work was a greater danger to the securtiy of the government of the United Kingdom than is the 'Ford strike to the security of the government of Canada. I was interested to see whether that Labour government would pass a law, and I was interested to find that they did not pass a law.

speechtext:
The Labour government said to the dockers, "We will be very glad to discuss your case after you have returned to work." I think that was a sound position to take and the only view that any government could take. If a government must form its legislation in the face of a strike, it is going to have very bad legislation indeed.
The labour legislation of Canada is advanced legislation. It has been well tried. We have machinery in this country to meet any situation. A great many crititical situations have been solved by the use of the labour legislation of this country. I think it is largely on account of that legislation that we have had fewer interruptions of labour in Canada than any other country on the side of the allies has had. Our difficulty is not lack of legislation; it is the unwillingness of the parties to a dispute to allow the labour legislation to operate. That is, the case in the Ford strike. The blame lies not on the one side or on the other; it lies on both sides to the dispute. We have found that both sides to the dispute have not cooperated with the government in allowing the machinery governing labour disputes to operate.
A great many lion, members have suggested that there is an easy way out of this situation; that is, to appoint a controller. Apparently that is the magic formula to solve any difficulty and remove any obstacle. I think I can claim to have invented the appointment of a controller to settle a labour dispute. I think the first appointment of the kind was made in the case of the National Steel Car strike in April, 1941. The National Steel-Car company was making 25-pounder shells,

Ford Motor Plant Strike
which were urgently needed at the front. It was one of the few munitions plants that Canada had in full production at that time. A series of labour disputes developed in the plant and resulted in one work stoppage, followed by a return to work and) a threatened further work stoppage. To straighten out the situation the government appointed a controller for that plant, quite an innovation at that time and one that was not at all welcomed either by labour or by the management.
Let me explain what appointing a controller means. The government in effect expropriates the property. We appointed that controller in the case of National Steel Car, knowing what we were doing and prepared to go through with it. We thought that the necessities of the case and the public interest involved warranted the government in taking that action and, if necessary, owning that property and paying the owners for it through the exchequer court. That possibility is always involved when the government steps in and takes over a business through the appointment of a controller. If the legislation has not sufficient teeth in it for that purpose, it is not an effective controllership. I do not think a government can bluff. If it appoints a controller it must be prepared to follow through to the logical outcome if that becomes necessary.
Subsequently to the National Steel Car situation we have appointed other controllers, but always when an issue of national interest was involved. We have appointed controllers in several war plants, always when there was a vital need for the output of the plant, and when the government felt that if the worst came to the worst it would be prepared to take over and operate the plant as a government property.
Recently controllers have been appointed in the packing industry. There, again, a great national issue was involved. The issue was, whether we were to carry out our commitments to Europe and especially to Great Britain, and as well assure our own people a proper supply of food. That was an issue of national interest which in my opinion warranted the appointment of a controller. If the result had been the ownership by the government of the packing house industry- and we were well aware that that might be the outcome-I still think the government was quite warranted in the step it took, even had that been the result.
It is proposed by some hon. gentlemen that we appoint a controller in the Ford dispute', which means in effect that we expropriate the Ford plant. I doubt very much that the government is in a position to operate a plant
manufacturing automobiles in a competitive market. I doubt whether there would1 be public support for a step of that kind. A good many may say: Well, you could take over the plant and make a few changes, and then the company will be glad to take it back again. I do not know whether they would be or. not. The company have not shown themselves inclined to act logically up to date, and I would not be a bit surprised if they would say: You have the plant, keep it and give us our 150,000,000 and you operate the plant.
