speechtext: You could say: Wait for the $50,000,000 for a while.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is a suggestion, but not very helpful. I can give my hou. friend an example of the appointment of a controller that should be interesting to him; I am speaking of a province which is the rnly province and the only government in the world that has legislation which provides by law the so-called union security that has been discussed. here to-night. I refer to Saskatchewan. There was a box factory in Prince Albert. This is a recent case, within the last two or three weeks. The factory employed some forty-five men. There was a dispute between management and employees, and the management was summoned to Regina under the drastic legislation of that province and ordered to set a certain schedule of wages. Management said that it could not operate on those wages. The province then threatened to appoint a controller. I do not know whether a controller was appointed, but I do know that in the course of a few days there were not any men working in that plant, and that the plant was closed. That can result under the most drastic legislation, and therefore I suggest that the answer is not to be found-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The government of
Saskatchewan has taken over that plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Perhaps they will know how
to make and sell boxes in competition. We will watch with interest. That is the logical outcome of a controllership, exactly what I have been saying. If we had drastic legislation here of a similar sort we might be taking over the Ford motor plant and be paying for it, because in a British country we never take property over without proper compensation. I do not think they will do otherwise in Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Again I ask: Is it a wise and prudent transaction for any government to undertake on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada? Perhaps no one is just as sure of the action that should be taken in this dispute
Ford Motor Plant Strike

as might appear from the speeches that we have heardl to-night. If I knew of any action that would end this dispute and not create more chaos in the labour situation than we have at this moment, I would certainly counsel my colleagues to adopt that course. Failing such knowledge, I think every effort must be made to resolve the dispute with the legislation that we have at this time. I do not think new legislation of any kind will help the situation. I think anything that can be done will be done in the next two or three days by the Minister of Labour on the spot in Windsor, and I can only ask hon. members in all sections of the house to refrain from making any statement or taking any action that will interfere with his efforts to that end.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been on my feet several times. I was attacked by a member of this house and I have a right to reply. I have risen more than once, and I protest against anything in the nature of discrimination.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member that I have the names here of members who have patiently been waiting for a chance to speak. The hon. member for Essex West and the hon. member for Winnipeg North have been waiting-for quite some time, and if the hon. member will permit the hon. member for Essex West to speak now, then so far as I am concerned he may have the floor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I was unaware that
there was a list when I spoke, or I might not have made the remark I just made. But, having been attacked, I think the list should be set aside in order that one might reply. That is the usual procedure in parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is discrimination.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I may say to the leader of the C.C.F. that if his colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North is willing to withdraw-this affects the bon. member for Essex West>-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I will yield my place to the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
As the representative of the constituency of Essex West I think I should say a few words, particularly since the dispute under discussion has as its location the city of Windsor, which comprises a chief part of my riding. I believe it is the duty of hon. members as Canadian statesmen to reconcile

the parties and heal the hurt of our people, not by the application of thorns and vinegar as evidenced in the comments of some who have taken part in the debate; for I sincerely believe that most parties represented in the house have a sincere desire to see that the present conditions are corrected.
I speak to-night on behalf of women and children as well as those men who are working in factories in the city of Windsor, people who have come from all parts of Canada and who by their initiative, their industry and their sincerity have built up the population of Windsor to approximately 130,000 in a comparatively few years. Those people, as their feelings are expressed in the telegram I hold in my hand, are in fear to-night. I believe that that fear is not well founded, for I am certain that I speak for all parties in saying that we desire to see that they are protected.
I am not going to discuss the issues involved in this dispute, because they have already been debated pro and con. The urgent matter, it seems to me, is the sending of force into the city of Windsor in the form of a certain number of dominion and provincial police. But at the outset I would like to say that I do not believe the use of force will cure the situation; it will not provide for us a lasting peace.	.
We have heard somewhat of social security. Social security is the coming together by common will of two individuals, one having confidence in the other, as we have had confidence in our own mothers and fathers. Until that condition is attained there will be no social security for it is a mental condition.
It has been represented that, because of the season of the year and imminent cold weather conditions, there may be some destruction of part of the plant of the Ford Motor company. Some machines which contain a certain amount of water might. be destroyed, and, if so, that plant will be closed for a year. I am not thinking of the company, but I am much concerned for our women and children, and for those workmen whose sole desire it is to provide for themselves and their families and to live in peace and contentment, who wish not to destroy but to produce. On behalf of these people I believe it our duty to do what we can to ensure that, their means of livelihood is protected. That it is at present endangered has been represented to me, and whether it is a fact or not I leave it to engineers to say. I have been informed that numbers of machines in this plant use a soda solution or a soap solution; that all these machines will have to be dismantled, reconditioned, and put together

Ford Motor Plant Strike
again, and that this process will take several weeks. Besides that, it has been represented to me that scores of electric motors will need to be reconditioned because they are now submerged in water. I do not know whether these statements are correct, but they have come to me from sources which I consider reliable. If these be the facts, we must do something to protect the livelihood of thousands of dependent men, women and children throughout the city.
It has been suggested that, in order to promote a settlement and get the plant in operation, the union permit the opening of the power plant and the return to work of members of the maintenance staff and persons engaged in the protective force. The strike could be allowed to continue, but at the same time there would be a voluntary arbitration, whereby the parties would consent to the appointment of an umpire. This would be done under the guidance of an umpire appointed by the government, whose decision would be final, and would be continued for a period of at least ten days, to a point which would permit the men to go back to work. If the union so requested, a commission might then be appointed to look into the question of annual wages with vacations. These proposals were submitted; I do not believe that they have been accepted.
If there are persons whose sole purpose it is to destroy, I am wholeheartedly opposed to them. If they want to destroy I am not with them. They are not the average workman; they are not the average citizen of the city of Windsor, because the citizen of Windsor is industrious. He wants to produce, but he is afraid and to-night he believes that the government, by the use of this force, is cooperating with the company in an attempt to break the strike. For that reason they are determined to fight. May I assure them that not only this government and the supporters of this government but, I feel sure, all members of this house will support me when I say that we are earnestly and sincerely trying to effect a settlement which will be to the benefit of these workers, that they need have no fear whatsoever, and that by reason of the facts which I have just stated it is essential that we protect the plant. I feel sure that with the means that have been taken even this day we can come to a reasonable settlement; for, after all, reasonable persons can come to harmonious and reasonable conclusions. I would say to the people of Windsor and environment that they need have no fear of any action of this government. I feel sure there will be no force used, because we are all determined, all mem-47696-118
bers of this house, to see that we get some solution of the problem which will heal the hurt of our people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I think everyone will agree with the hon. member for Essex West that the people who suffer most in the strike are usually the wives and children of the workers and the workers themselves. After all, a great corporation can hold out almost indefinitely; all that is disturbing is that the plant is idle and may deteriorate in some respects. But the women and children, the wives of the workers and the workers themselves have to provide a place in which to live and to try to live decently. They have to eat. Consequently anyone who has a semblance of humanitarianism in him is anxious to see the settlement of a dispute of this description.
I am interested in this strike because it is the first of the great post-war strikes that we may encounter unless we have either provincial or federal machinery-or both-to deal with them. The Minister of Reconstruction made a constructive speech this evening. He pointed out the long experience he has had with labour himself and the success he has had in dealing with unions, and he went on to speak of the union situation in Great Britain, where conditions are not comparable with those in this country. In Great Britain for the last fifty years the unions have been well established. The unions have gained that recognition which enlightened employers like the Minister of Reconstruction have accorded them in this country. But unfortunately in Canada we have had a different situation. The unions in Canada have been fought tooth and nail by corporations like the Ford Company and others of the same stamp.
One of the interesting features of this debate to-night is that nobody has dared to rise in his place and say a single word on behalf of Henry Ford or the Ford corporation. I have listened, and not one individual member of this house has dared to rise in his place and say a solitary single word in defence of Ford or his corporation. That in itself is a striking condemnation on the part of parliament of the Ford way of doing business.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is not a question of daring to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I will put it in another way. It is not a question of daring to, the hon. member says. Well, no one has found any reason to rise in this house and say one word in favour of Ford, and if my hon. friend has a reason I suggest that he tell the committee what his reason is for having respect for Ford or his corporation.

Ford Motor Plant Strike

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It would not be because I do not dare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is all right. I suggest that if the hon. member has a reason he should state it and not hide it under his bushel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Do not accuse members of this house of not daring.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The minister said that eighty-five per cent of' the workers of the Ford plant would be employed if this strike had not occurred. Then what is it that has brought about the strike? Fear-fear of the ultimate loss of employment; fear of the loss of even that semblance of union security, if I may use the term, which the workers of that company and of other companies have won during this war. Fear is at the base of the present labour situation in this country as it is in connection with this company.
The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), when he reads his speech tomorrow, will be surprised at some of the things he said. He began by arguing against compulsory membership in unions, compulsory unions and compulsory check-off, attacking us because we had suggested that in our speeches to-day; and he wound up by trying to contend that the compulsory check-off, compulsory union and enforcement by legislation was the policy he was suggesting. When he reads his speech to-morrow morning-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman,-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am not attacking the hon. member as he attacked us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The hon. member did not listen to my speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I listened to the speech;
I believe I have average intelligence to interpret it, and if the hon. member ^ill use the same intelligence to-morrow morning when he reads it he will reach the conclusion I have just reached.
When he says that we have made no constructive suggestions, I would point out that for many years, because of the industrial situation in this country, we have advocated the establishment of a national labour code. We have urged that provincial-dominion conferences should be held in order that agreement might be reached with the provinces, so that we might know where the power lies, with a view to adopting a proper labour code in Canada. During this war we have urged that when, under the emergency power, the govern-
ment passes an order in council dealing with labour matters it should deal not only' with the workers' obligations but, in the same manner should compel industry or the employers to institute collective bargaining.
The weakness of P.C. 1003, as everyone knows, is that it expresses a pious hope and says that something should be done, but it does not provide the means of making sure that it shall be done. We have suggested three things: 1. That a controller should be put into this plant pending a negotiated settlement. 2. That the police should be withdrawm. 3. That there should be legislation to bring about satisfactory union conditions for the workers. These three things we have suggested; they have been suggested in other parts of the house, sometimes separately, sometimes collectively, and sometimes the persons suggesting them were not awTare that they were making such proposals. I say to the Acting Prime Minister that when he says that we are supporting illegality he knows that cannot be substantiated by facts. Throughout the whole of our existence we have stood for law and order; but there are times when disorder has been provoked by government action.
My hon. friend the member for Vancouver-Burrard sits to-day wearing the political stripe of a party which has one of the worst labour records of any political party in the British commonwealth of nations. I am not forgetting that after the last war the former leader of this group, my predecessor, was arrested in Winnipeg; his colleagues were arrested in Winnipeg, and the leader of the Conservative party at that time wired to Winnipeg, when it was pointed out to him that the arrests and what was proposed to be done with those arrested were illegal, and said: "Carry out my instructions; I will legalize them afterwards."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Shame!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We do not want a repetition of that kind of thing in this country. Let me say this, too, nor do we want a repetition of the kind of thing that happened in the depression. I remember Regina in 1935 and Mr. Bennett's iron heel. I remember how the mounted police there provoked disorder by throwing tear gas bombs into a citizens' meeting, not a meeting solely of the trekkers who were in the city at the time, and thus brought about a condition whereby they could drive those young men out of the city and prevent their march to Ottawa. I may say to my hon. friends opposite, the same kind of thing happened in 1938, under their administration, in the Vancouver post office. We do not

Ford Motor Plant Strike
want to see a repetition of that kind of thing.
When you talk about supporting illegality, who provokes it? That is the point. Who provokes it? I say that this situation which we have in Windsor to-night is due to the inaction of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Provoked by inaction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard talks about referring this matter to the industrial relations committee of this house. All I can say is, the best thing he can do is to read the evidence that was given before the national war labour board in regard to these matters, and then read its report of 1943, and he will find therein a complete and full investigation of everything that he proposes to investigate anew.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I doubt that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
may doubt it, but I would suggest that he read it first and then express any doubts that he may have after he has read the report. That is the time to express doubt about it. Therefore I say that if this strike is to be settled you will have to remove the cause of the strike, and the cause of the strike, as everybody who has spoken to-day has, by implication at least, admitted, is the management of the Ford company at Windsor. There is a different management at Detroit and there are different conditions. The very things that the men are fighting for in Windsor have been granted across the river in Detroit. Why? Because the Canadian management of the Ford company is at fault. It is all very well for members to rise in this house and say that we must not take sides. There are occasions when by not taking sides you are taking a side. I make no apologies for taking a side.	I am on the side of the men,
definitely, because I believe the fault over the years lies with the .company. I know, as I am sure the members who represent Windsor and the Essex county seats in this house know, the whole story of the long years of antiunionism of the management of the Canadian Ford company. The same thing applied in Detroit, the only difference being that in Detroit they got rid of it a little earlier and the United States has a labour code.
On our side of the line the story - is writ large in the misery of a good many men who tried to work for their fellowmen in the Ford corporation throughout the years. As has been said, this dates back not one month, two months, seventeen months, but years. The time has come when, if I may use the same expression as the hon. member for Vancouver-
Burrard used, we should grasp the nettle and grasp it tightly. But the nettle you have to grasp is the management of the Ford corporation in Canada. The only way that you can deal with the corporation at the moment is to show that you mean business. To put in a controller does not mean that you are to socialize the plant immediately. It does not mean that you are taking it out of the ownership of those who own it to-day, but you are taking it out of the control of those who now exercise it: Mr. Campbell and the group of Ford owners whom he represents; that is all.
May I say this, too, I believe that with a controller in the plant and the men going back into the plant, the workers who are in the managerial positions in the plant would be happier men; for no man, whether he was a humble worker on the assembly line or a man who does an important, job at the managerial end, can be happy under the conditions that have existed and continue to exist in the Ford plant.
This is a test for the government, or if you will, it is a test for this house because, if you take the situation at Windsor which we are emphasizing and look a little farther afield, you will see what I mean. Look at the situation around Guelph and learn something about the sinister figures who are responsible for the conditions there and then see where they are going to lead us in a little while, if they are allowed to continue. I do not want to divert attention from Windsor to Guelph, but one of these days soon some inquiry will have to be made regarding the situation at Guelph, and in the meantime some understanding should be attempted as to what is behind the situation there.
Let me come back to the Ford situation again. We suggest at this time .that there is one thing that the government can do, and one thing only, namely, to appoint a controller, to withdraw provocation in the form of the police. Let me say that I have received a protest to-day, not from any strikers, not from people who I thought sympathized with the men on strike in the Ford plant, against the Royal Canadian Air Force planes being used to transport the police to Windsor. But I see it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
